POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 19:19:56 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Croatian MEP stands down from national party after friends and family attended EU Parliament event  https://www.politico.eu/article/croatia-mep-romana-jerkovic-stand-down-national-party-friends-family-european-parliament-event/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 18:02:35 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9130925 A Croatian MEP stood down from her national party on Thursday after POLITICO revealed her inner circle attended a taxpayer-funded European Parliament event in Strasbourg.

Romana Jerković, who sits with the Socialists and Democrats group in the European Parliament, was to face a disciplinary investigation by her SDP party in Croatia. The party leader, Siniša Hajdaš Dončić, said he wanted the SDP presidency to open a disciplinary proceeding with the intention of excluding the MEP.

Before the meeting, due Thursday, Jerković announced she was leaving the party.

“I am not leaving because I have done anything for which I should have to justify myself or feel ashamed,” she said in a press release.

“Just like all other MEPs, I invited citizens to Parliament whom I was entitled to invite —individuals whose experience and work directly contributed to the health policies we were developing. All rules were followed, including transparent reporting to the competent institutions, which confirmed that there were no irregularities,” the MEP said.

POLITICO cited documents showing that some of Jerković’s friends and family — including an art historian acquaintance and an actor friend — attended a health policy event organized by the lawmaker in December 2024, with their flights and meals paid for by the Socialists and Democrats group.

An attendance list seen by POLITICO showed these people had signed up for the event as doctors and medical academics. Jerković said this was an “admin error,” and that the S&D had no issues with her conduct. The S&D said it had rechecked the relevant documents and had concluded “the related financial rules were respected.”

“That is why I am not prepared to accept having my professional integrity judged based on insinuations, fabrications, and smear tactics. One set of rules cannot apply to me while another applies to others,” she said in the statement.

SDP Secretary-General Jure Zubčić also released a statement, saying: “We must set a new bar for standards in Croatian politics. Accountability is not limited to liability for misdemeanours or criminal offences. There is also political and moral accountability. Anyone who crosses that line will, unfortunately, have no place in SDP.”

NATO announced Thursday that 17 allies will participate in the annual Steadfast Noon exercise from Oct. 13-23. But this year, the exercise follows a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after allies conducted exercises near Russia’s Kaliningrad exclave in August.

“We have been doing this every year and … this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry,” said Nassima Barrows, NATO’s nuclear policy director. “This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate.”

“Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability,” she told reporters.

Following the previous NATO exercises, Moscow sent a letter to the alliance threatening to hit allied territory and mentioning the use of its nuclear arsenal — a move that NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte publicly rebuked last week.

Tensions are rising as European countries accuse Russia of sabotage and growing so-called hybrid attacks across the continent. 

“Our intention is to really keep things calm,” said a senior NATO official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. Russian officials “keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood.”

U.S. Col. David Bull, chief of NATO’s nuclear operations, said the exercise has garnered “similar” participation to previous years and involves everything from a “simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise” — but “no live nuclear weapons.” 

It will also feature dual-capable aircraft and ground troops to support the exercise and train on loading, fueling, and maintaining planes, a senior NATO military official added.

Russia’s embassy to Belgium didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

]]> en French top general acknowledges joint tank program with Germany has failed https://www.politico.eu/article/french-top-general-acknowledges-franco-german-tank-program-failed/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:37:30 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9131015 PARIS — France’s top general Fabien Mandon admitted on Thursday that the Franco-German next-generation battle tank project had failed.

It’s one of the first times a French official has publicly acknowledged that the plans have faltered, after months of speculation about the fate of the Main Combat Ground System.

“The outcome isn’t good. We had hoped to build a future tank in cooperation with the Germans, but unfortunately, we have to acknowledge that the Germans have withdrawn from the project,” the French chief of defense staff told lawmakers during a hearing on next year’s budget.

MGCS — which involves KNDS France, KNDS Germany, Rheinmetall and Thales — has been bogged down by years of delays, industrial disputes and political tensions. POLITICO reported in June that the next-generation tank project was increasingly doomed.

Mandon’s admission comes only a few months after another high-stakes Franco-German defense industrial program — the Future Combat Air System — abruptly ended.

However, answering a question from a far-right National Rally lawmaker, the French general pushed back against the word “failure” to describe the MGCS’s fate.

“It’s not a complete failure; it’s an important decision by Germany, but our land forces have worked together for several years to determine what a future main battle tank should look like,” he said. “It wasn’t a waste of time. But from an industrial standpoint, this isn’t good news.”

A German defense official had no comment.

Rixa Fürsen contributed to this report.

]]> en UK plans to announce ban on workers’ non-compete clauses in push for growth https://www.politico.eu/article/uk-plans-to-announce-ban-on-workers-non-compete-clauses-in-push-for-growth/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:34:20 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9131312 LONDON — The U.K. government is planning to commit to a full or partial ban on non-compete clauses in workers’ employment contracts, six people with knowledge of the discussions told POLITICO.

All six of the people, who were granted anonymity to discuss government policy, said they believed an announcement is due imminently and could be made as soon as Friday. Three of those people said they believed the announcement was likely to be fronted personally by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is expected to give a speech Friday.

The government of Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, set out options in November 2025 to limit the use of non-compete clauses, which aim to restrict a person’s ability to work for or set up a competing business after they leave their job.

The founders of more than 20 U.K. tech start-ups wrote to the government last month saying the restrictions, along with long notice periods and enforced gardening leave, were and “undermin[ing] the innovation that drives economic growth”.

The options set out 11 months ago ranged from a total ban on non-compete clauses to a partial ban, such as allowing non-compete clauses only for workers earning more than a set salary threshold, or limiting their length.

However, two of the six people quoted above said that the government would stop short of backing a specific option at this stage.

Ministers are expected to set out a broad intention of ensuring that non-compete clauses are no longer a hiring problem for start-ups and innovative firms, but finer details will be worked out further down the line in consultation with industry.

No. 10 declined to comment.

The announcement comes after Chancellor John Healey said he wanted to tackle the costs for businesses in his budget on Oct. 28. One of the six people quoted above said: “They want to sell it as pro growth and freeing up the labour market.”

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the government was “working extremely rapidly” on potential changes to the system.

Non-compete clauses are common in the financial services industry. The lobby group TheCityUK opposed a ban earlier this year, arguing that non-compete clauses “promote competition and innovation in high-value industries” as they are often the “only way to pre-emptively protect confidential information and intellectual property.”

The government argued last year that even though non-compete clauses are “unenforceable” as a starting point under current law, ministers were “concerned about the behavioural effect of including a non-compete clause in an employment contract. Even if broadly drafted and unlikely to be enforceable, workers may perceive the clause as binding and comply with it for fear of legal repercussions.”

]]> fr Burnham signals ‘openness’ to Germany joining GCAP fighter jet program https://www.politico.eu/article/burnham-signals-openness-to-germany-joining-jet-fighter-program/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:57:16 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9130082 Britain is open to Germany joining the sixth-generation jet fighter Global Combat Air Programme led by the U.K., Italy and Japan, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Thursday.

“I’ve indicated to the chancellor in our discussion… our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham said in Berlin during a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

“That is something we seek to progress in the coming period working with our other partners Italy and Japan in relation to that as well,” he added.

POLITICO reported last month that Berlin has held exploratory talks about participating in GCAP after Germany’s combat aircraft plans with France collapsed earlier this year.

“This is neither a decision nor a preliminary decision. It is a first, small step in Germany’s efforts to seek—and possibly find—partnerships in this area,” said a senior German official, who spoke on condition of being granted anonymity.

“We are at a very early stage in reassessing our options. Germany has not made a decision yet. It is exploring all possible avenues,” they said. “However, you are aware of the chancellor’s position that he favors a European solution rather than Germany acting alone.”

Earlier this year, Canada became the first observer nation in GCAP, which could be a pathway to full future membership. Other possible members include Saudi Arabia.

However, the three GCAP members have been wary of opening the club, worrying about less work for each partner nation or delays to the program.

The CEO of Italian defense firm Leonardo, which is part of the GCAP industrial coalition within the program, said in July that if another country wants to join the program, it needs to happen within the next 12 months.

The British leader also outlined a new partnership with Germany to counter hybrid threats from countries such as Russia.

“The defense ministries have been tasked with exploring ways to expand this partnership,” said the German official.

]]> en Germany wants UK to raise tariffs on Chinese EVs https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-uk-raise-tariff-china-electric-vehicle/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:15:20 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9127871 LONDON — Germany wants the U.K. to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in exchange for protection from Made in Europe rules, according to a person familiar with Berlin’s position.

Friedrich Merz’s government believes the move would show reciprocity on trade and counter accusations from other EU member states that Britain is trying to “cherry pick” the benefits of EU membership, said the person, who was granted anonymity to discuss closed-door talks.

It comes as Prime Minister Andy Burnham met with the German chancellor on his first official visit to the country this week.

Burnham and Merz were due to talk about possibilities for Britain’s future relationship with the EU — after the British prime minister put rejoining the bloc back on the table of U.K. politics for the first time in a decade.

Berlin’s position on EV tariffs is significant as Germany has broadly backed a tolerant policy towards the U.K. on trade matters since Brexit — in contrast to more hard-line positions taken by countries like France.

The EU is in the process of drawing up new Made in Europe rules that would favor European producers over those outside the bloc — in response to trade practices by competitors like China and the United States.

The U.K. is worried that the measures will hit British business — especially automakers — and wants assurances from Brussels that it will get an opt out. If Berlin gets its way, those assurances could be dependent on emulating EU trade policy with regard to Chinese EVs.

Predatory strategy

Germany’s vaunted car industry, arguably the jewel in the country’s economic crown, has faced stiff competition from Chinese imports in recent years.

EU countries have accused China of dumping low-cost, state-subsidized electric vehicles into the European market and in December 2024 imposed countervailing duties as high as 35.3. percent on some manufacturers.

Industry Commissioner Stephane Séjourné accused China of pursuing a deliberate “predatory strategy” with state subsidies to the tune of €10,000 per vehicle.

The U.K.’s Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told POLITICO last month that the government was keeping tariffs “under review, to be frank, more closely than lots of other issues” and that “different parts of our own sector want different things from” the government’s policy.

Hamish Falconer, the U.K.’s minister for European relations, told POLITICO’s Brussels Playbook Podcast this week that he was “surprised” at reports tariffs might be a condition of Made in Europe opt-outs, adding: “That’s not the kind of conversation that I’m having with my European counterparts.”

Going ahead with higher tariffs risks alienating Beijing, which has expressed serious concerns about the policy. It would also raise the price of electric vehicles on the market, potentially making it harder for the government to meet its decarbonization targets.

]]> en China trade talks test EU’s appetite for tougher action https://www.politico.eu/article/china-trade-talks-eu-appetite-tougher-action/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:05:36 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9128789 BRUSSELS — European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič opened two days of talks in Beijing on Thursday aimed at rebalancing a gaping trade deficit, with failure to reach a deal likely to test Brussels’ resolve to impose tougher trade restrictions.

The meeting marks the final round of an effort launched in June to reset the lopsided trading relationship, and will hinge on whether China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is prepared to make substantial concessions.

If no agreement can be reached to narrow the EU’s €1 billion-a-day goods trade deficit, Brussels and Beijing could find themselves on a collision course. EU leaders will review the outcome of the talks at a summit in Brussels next Thursday, where they will consider next steps.

Arriving in China, Šefčovič said his goal was to balance what he called an unsustainable trade deficit. Heading into a meeting with Wang, he said it was crucial that the talks deliver “tangible outcomes.”

The discussions have zeroed in on cars, with Chinese exports increasingly eating into the market share of European automakers. In August, one in eight cars bought in the bloc was Chinese, thanks largely to a boom in sales of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.

European negotiators have been pushing China to commit to some form of export restraint — in particular for hybrids. Unlike Chinese-made battery-electric vehicles, which were hit with extra countervailing duties in 2024, plug-in hybrids are not subject to such measures.

Without meaningful commitments from Beijing, the Commission has warned it will resort to unilateral trade restrictions. For cars, it is considering safeguard measures that would mix import quotas and tariffs to protect European automakers.

Chemicals are next. Industry Commissioner Stéphane Séjourné said Thursday that the Commission plans to introduce targeted safeguards on plastics and composite materials, subject to a request from EU governments that Brussels do so.

Wind in his sails 

Šefčovič flew to Beijing with the backing of the leaders of Europe’s two biggest economies — France and Germany — to take a tougher approach to trade.

In a joint appeal on Monday, President Emmanuel Macron and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Commission should be given a freer hand to shut off access to the EU for goods from countries that distort the bloc’s single market.

While the two leaders did not mention China in their letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, there was no mistaking the target of their proposed trade “kill switch,” which could be blocked only by a qualified majority of EU countries.

The EU already has a powerful trade weapon in its Anti-Coercion Instrument, designed to counter economic bullying by foreign powers. 

But Brussels has yet to muster broad support from member countries to deploy it, most recently in January when U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to seize Greenland, a Danish territory.

The EU’s difficulty in responding swiftly to trade threats has heightened concerns about a surge in Chinese exports that European officials say benefit from unfair government subsidies. With Trump hiking U.S. tariffs, ever more Chinese exports are heading to Europe — increasing pressure on industries that are already being forced to retrench.

Europe’s heavy dependence on China for processed rare earths and other critical raw materials also leaves it vulnerable to retaliation should relations deteriorate.

“If we aren’t willing to fix the way our model works, then we’ll be destroyed,” said one EU diplomat, summing up the concerns flooding Brussels.

“What’s the point of having [more tools] if the Chinese can shut down our strategic production in a matter of days?”

Low expectations

Although Šefčovič entered the talks strengthened by the Franco-German letter, a second diplomat said they didn’t foresee a deal with Beijing this week.

“He knows that a lot of member states are behind the Franco-German push,” the diplomat said, adding that this “has been seen in China.” 

But Beijing has little room to compromise, given its reliance on exports to sustain growth amid weak domestic demand and a prolonged property slump.

“The Chinese side is starting to recognize that there is a problem. But I don’t think they are ready to enter into a substantial deal,” said Gunnar Wiegand, a former head of the EU diplomatic service’s Asia-Pacific department.

Wiegand, now a visiting fellow at the German Marshall Fund, said Šefčovič had earned a reputation as a dealmaker in talks on Britain’s exit from the EU and in last year’s trade deal with Trump. This time, however, “both sides are bound by their own circumstances,” he said.

Europe is desperate to halt the erosion of its industrial base, while China remains heavily dependent on exports to sustain economic growth. 

“The Chinese are going to object to being singled out. Even if a deal with the EU would be the most rational solution, other important markets for Chinese exports, such as ASEAN countries, will start asking the same. It will undercut their global market,” he said. 

]]> en ‘Targets of terror’: Russia kills 33 in single strike in Donbas https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-kills-30-civilians-single-strike-donbas-ukraine/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:48:56 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9128204 KYIV — At least 33 people were killed and 22 injured in a Russian attack on two buses in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donbas region Thursday morning, local authorities said.

“At the time of the attack, civilian buses were carrying passengers. People just going by their day,” Kramatorsk city council said in a statement. “For frontline Kramatorsk — where only a fraction of the population remains due to constant Russian shelling and evacuations — every trip across the city is an inherent daily risk. There are few people left here. Yet, even civilian vehicles carrying passengers become targets of Russian terror,” the city council added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said doctors were “fighting to save the lives of people injured” and that the number of fatalities may still rise. “Some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries. My condolences to all their families and loved ones,” he added. Prosecutors have opened a criminal case into the attack.

“This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response — exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought,” Zelenskyy added.

In an interview Thursday, U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio said that currently “there does not seem to be any prospect of a negotiated settlement … as the Russians are making a condition of full control of Donetsk, which Ukraine rejects as unacceptable.”

Russia has claimed that a key objective of its invasion is to save the Russian-speakers of Donbas from “genocide conducted by Ukraine,” with President Vladimir Putin saying on Oct. 1 his country would “liberate” Donbas much sooner than Ukraine expects. Moscow has so far issued no statement on the latest strike, but has repeatedly denied targeting Ukrainian civilians.

This latest strike comes just a day after Russia’s missile strike on a residential building in Pryluky killed 22 and injured more than 50. Since August, Moscow has launched a wave of retaliatory attacks in response to Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries and marketplaces.

This article was updated.

]]> en Slovakia’s Fico calls nude Trump statue a sign of EU decline https://www.politico.eu/article/slovakia-robert-fico-nude-donald-trump-statue-orange-plague-european-parliament/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:08:45 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9128051 Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico on Thursday called for the removal of a satirical statue of U.S. President Donald Trump from the European Parliament, describing it as a “sign of the decline of the entire European Union.”

Writing on X, Fico said that while he does not agree with all of Trump’s policies, “insulting our partners on official premises demonstrates a profound failure to understand the times we live in.”

The sculpture, titled The Orange Plague, was unveiled Tuesday by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt in the Parliament building in Strasbourg. The 2.6-meter work depicts a nude, gold-leaf-covered Trump perched on a frail man’s shoulders, holding a golf club and scales of justice. A plaque reads: “I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden.”

“It is sad that the leadership of the European Parliament, in its blindness, can no longer distinguish between the legitimate right to hold a different opinion and the actions of spiritually bankrupt individuals, adventurers and lunatics,” Fico added, before asking whether the Parliament would tolerate similar depictions of the French president or German chancellor.

The statue was removed on Wednesday, a spokesperson for the European Parliament said after publication. It was part of a two-day exhibition at the initiative of Danish left-wing MEP Per Clausen.

POLITICO was present at the unveiling, where visitors clamored for miniature replicas of the sculpture, which were distributed in several colors. The statue stands in a prominent spot at the entrance to Parliament’s Winston Churchill building, before the corridor linking MEPs’ and Commission officials’ offices with the plenary chamber.

Galschiøt said the work was intended to confront Trump’s policies and start a debate about how the U.S. president was “destroying the world’s only chance to counter the climate catastrophe.”

Clausen defended the installation in a statement. “If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture … then they have no place on the world stage,” he said.

“MEPs have the possibility to hold cultural events/ exhibitions in the European Parliament … These cultural events and exhibitions by Members shall be authorised in advance by the Quaestors who assess the compliance with the rules in place,” the European Parliament press service said in a statement to POLITICO.

“The rules in place outline that cultural events and exhibitions shall under no circumstances be offensive or of an inflammatory nature or contradictory to the values on which the Union is founded or likely to give rise to disturbances in the designated exhibition areas,” the statement says.

Fico has cultivated ties with Trump, meeting him at Mar-a-Lago in January to discuss closer cooperation, including civilian nuclear energy. He has praised the MAGA movement as “a vision that urgently resonates not only in the United States but across the world.”

The sculpture was previously displayed at protests in Copenhagen and the COP30 summit in Brazil. It is due to appear at next month’s COP31 conference in Antalya, Türkiye.

Trump has not commented on the installation.

Gerardo Fortuna contributed to this report. This article was updated.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:50:43 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 EU Parliament’s 7 October memorial honours Israelis, sidelines Palestinians — and sows division https://euobserver.com/241740/eu-parliaments-7-october-memorial-honours-israelis-sidelines-palestinians-and-sows-division/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241740 A memorial to victims of 7 October in Israel, which made no mention of Palestinian casualties, ended in tumbling flags, anger, and grief. ]]> An EU Parliament memorial for victims of the 7 October attack caused disarray and anger as well as grief in a divided European house.

It was crowned by a towering Israeli flag, alongside the EU’s.

The exhibit set up in Strasbourg’s parliament included maps showing Occupied Palestinian Territories as part of Israel and sold trinkets made from debris of Israeli missiles.

But the Kremlin has said there is nothing to see.]]> First published in Respekt, adapted by EUobserver

Unsavoury news comes from Russia country often these days. But the latest unexpected development is the spread of a deadly disease.

Behind the mysterious death of a young woman in Siberia in early October was reportedly pneumonic plague – a disease so contagious it is considered as bad as anthrax, smallpox, and Ebola.

Local authorities in Russia have denied the plague as cause of death, but despite this, they have implemented anti-epidemic measures.

Eva Hrncirova, a spokesperson for the European Commission, said on Thursday (8 October): “Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible. This is what we need”.

“We had a meeting with the member states yesterday within the [EU Commission’s] Health Security Committee, and with the WHO [World Health Organization], who are in contact with our delegation in Moscow,” she said.

Russia was asked by the WHO to share “timely, precise, and exact information” about the possible plague in Siberia, she also said.

“We don’t have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation,” she added.

Nothing to see here, says Russia

Pneumonic plague disease can be treated with antibiotics if detected early, but officials beyond Russia’s borders are left with worrying questions.

Did an Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute lab technician in Shelekhov (Siberia) really die of plague?

If so, was it a natural version of the disease, or a more dangerous bacterium modified in military labs?

And what is the risk of the Middle Ages-era disease spreading?

Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis — the same one that once brought devastating plague epidemics known as the Black Death.

The pneumonic form of plague, a disease that killed up to half of Europe’s population in the 14th century, spreads through droplets by coughing or sneezing.

It manifests as severe, rapidly developing pneumonia that almost always ends in death if left untreated. But if antibiotics are administered in time (ideally within 24 hours of the onset of symptoms), the disease is treatable.

Independent Russian-language media say that Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old laboratory technician at the research and hygiene institute in question, accidentally broke a test tube containing plague bacteria in late September, became infected and died in hospital several days later, on 2 October.

Authorities have not confirmed the cause of the woman’s death, letting on only that she died of pneumonia and claiming that no microorganisms connected with her work had been found in her body.

Some 200 of her contacts were subsequently put into quarantine with medical supervision.

Authorities also ordered a three-week quarantine at several hospitals in the wider area, and facemasks for the wider population – even for schoolchildren.

Read more

EU has ‘learned nothing’ from Covid say MEPs, as mpox outbreak grows

Russia’s neighbours, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, have all introduced border controls.

Russia said the epidemic situation in the area was stable, that none of the deceased woman’s contacts had shown signs of infection, and that there was no cause for concern.

However, the head of Russia’s public health authority reportedly travelled to Irkutsk to attend a meeting with local officials, while residents of Shelekhov report that people in protective suits are moving around the town.

And epidemiologists say it is simply not possible that Russia’s public health service would resort to such dramatic measures, including closing hospitals, over a single case of ‘pneumonia of unknown origin’ .

The institute where the laboratory technician worked is said to be a civilian facility that, among other things, researches and monitors the incidence of plague.

In Siberia, especially near the borders with China and Mongolia, the bacteria in question still circulate among animals and occasionally infect humans, as they do in some parts of Africa, where the disease is most common.

    ]]>         Morocco’s surveillance state does not stop at Western Sahara — and Europe can no longer pretend not to know https://euobserver.com/241454/moroccos-surveillance-state-does-not-stop-at-western-sahara-and-europe-can-no-longer-pretend-not-to-know/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 08:50:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241454 As new evidence emerges of Moroccan spying on Sahrawi activists, including in Europe, European governments continue to deepen their security ties with Rabat without seriously questioning how those capabilities are being used.]]> In April 2021, I told The Guardian that Sahrawi activists were having their phones and internet connections hacked.

    At the time, we could describe what was happening to us. We could not see the machinery behind it.

    Five years later, Amnesty International’s new investigation, “We Start With the Verdict”: Inside Morocco’s Surveillance Machine, gives those warnings a disturbing new context.

    Amnesty describes a surveillance ecosystem involving spyware, physical surveillance, location tracking, informants, judicial pressure and smear campaigns. Western Sahara is not peripheral to its findings.

    The organisation devotes a case study to Sahrawi activists and reports that a former member of Morocco’s domestic intelligence service, identified as “Safir,” described Sahrawis and Riffians as priority intelligence targets, including beyond Morocco.     The report also contains forensic evidence involving Pegasus spyware and documents cases connected to Sahrawi activism that reached European territory.

    The people Amnesty examined are the tip of the iceberg. They are documented cases: people researchers could interview, devices they could examine, or targets for whom other evidence was available.

    Surveillance is secret by design. Most people never learn that their phones have been compromised, and most suspicious devices will never reach a forensic laboratory.

    That is why the chronology matters.

    Chilling effect

    On 8 April 2021, The Guardian quoted my warning that Sahrawi activists’ “phones and internet connections are hacked.” We were describing the symptoms years before Amnesty’s latest investigation exposed more of the machinery.

    But surveillance is not simply about collecting information.

    When a security service knows who an activist speaks to, where that person travels and what exists inside a phone, information can become power.

    Amnesty documents cases in which private information gathered through surveillance later appeared in media coverage and coordinated smear campaigns against human rights defenders.

    The organisation is careful: it could not independently establish the source of every piece of private material published. But it says the nature of some material raises serious concerns that surveillance-derived information may have reached media actors.

    For Sahrawis, that raises an obvious question: How does private information about activists move from their lives and devices into the public sphere?

    That question deserves independent forensic investigation.

    But Amnesty’s report should provoke another examination — this one in Washington and European capitals.

    For decades, Western governments have built close security relationships with Morocco around counterterrorism, intelligence cooperation, migration and regional stability.

    The question is not whether those relationships should exist. It is whether the West has adequately examined what happens to security capabilities once they are in the hands of its partners.

It was an ordinary five-storey building. Unfortunately, according to current information, five people were killed and 26 injured, including five children. People may still be trapped beneath the rubble,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

    The Russian attack damaged five apartment blocks in Dnipro and four in the city of Kremenchuk. This is what the situation in Kremenchuk looked like.

    Overall, according to Zelensky, at least 11 people were killed and dozens were injured.

    As can be seen in these photographs, a ballistic missile fell in Kyiv but did not explode; Ukrainian bomb disposal experts tried to render it harmless.

    Chart of the day

    Ukrainians claim that their attacks on refineries have put more than 50 percent of Russia’s oil-processing capacity out of action. Michael Bohnert, an analyst at the RAND think tank, wrote on X that this was not entirely accurate. According to his calculations, current fuel production at Russian refineries stands at 3.22 million barrels per day. Before the war, it was usually around 5.5 million barrels per day, meaning a fall of about 40 percent.

    There has also been a monthly decline of 0.36 million barrels per day, apparently owing to the latest attacks on refineries, for example in Moscow and Samara.

    According to Bohnert, this is the third time Ukrainians have managed to reduce Russian oil processing so substantially. There was a drop of around 40 percent last autumn and in July this year. “3.2m barrels per day is roughly the point at which things start becoming uncomfortable for Moscow,” he wrote.

    Unlike last year, however, Russia is helping itself through imports. The country, once the world’s third-largest fuel exporter, has sharply curtailed its exports. At the same time, it is partially making up for the shortfall in domestic production through imports.

    South Korea is also helping it in this respect. According to information from the Guardian, 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mainly diesel, arrived from South Korea at Russian ports in the Far East in July and August. Seven tankers made a total of 14 voyages to Russia. Three of the tankers are on the European Union’s sanctions list.

    Overall, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of petroleum products by sea in August, a third of them from South Korea. The country, which once supported Ukraine not only verbally but also through non-military aid, is now helping Russia cope with Ukrainian attacks on refineries.

    High petrol prices are also working in Russia’s favour. Analysts at the Kyiv School of Economics Institute published a chart showing that Russia exported the least oil and petroleum products in August since 2018. As the final bar in the left-hand chart shows, this was mainly due to a decline in petroleum-product exports.

    Nevertheless, revenue from sales remains at last year’s level (the purple line in the left-hand chart). This is mainly due to the rise in their prices on global markets as a result of the US-Israeli war against Iran.

    Videos of the day

    This was the sunset seen by residents of the Russian coastal city of Sochi on Tuesday. A tanker sailing under the Liberian flag was burning close to shore. Footage showed that it was ablaze along virtually its entire length.

    The Russian Rybar channel wrote that it had been hit by naval drones. It was therefore probably a Ukrainian attack on Russia’s shadow fleet, which exports oil around the world and thereby finances the war.

    The oil-laden tanker was travelling from Novorossiysk to India. Local residents reported an explosion and feared that oil would spill into the sea.

    This is a rather surreal continuation of the previous video. A man is playing guitar on the promenade in Sochi while an oil tanker burns behind him, sending up an enormous plume of smoke.

    Ukrainians are experimenting with remotely controlled vehicles. This video shows how a US Humvee off-road vehicle was converted into a remotely operated ground drone. It was loaded with wooden beams, which it delivered to soldiers building fortifications.

    This video shows a duel between a Ukrainian robot and a Russian FPV drone. In this case, the robot ultimately won, neutralising the drone by ramming it.

    Ukrainian attacks on the land route to Crimea continue. This is what one of the roads to Crimea currently looks like, with numerous damaged and destroyed lorries visible.

    What are the losses

    No update on Wednesday.

    • By Monday (5 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,170 pieces of heavy equipment (24,138 on Tuesday, 22 September). Of these, 19,133 (19,105) were destroyed by Ukrainians, 1,003 (1,000) were damaged, 1,194 (1,194) were abandoned by their crews, and 2,840 (2,839) were captured by the Ukrainian army. This includes 4,452 (4,448) tanks, of which 3,357 (3,353) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine has lost 12,238 (12,175) pieces of equipment, of which 9,633 (9,579) were destroyed, 711 (702) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. This includes 1,466 (1,464) tanks, of which 1,126 (1,125) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its fatalities or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list of equipment losses documented exclusively by photographs since the start of the war.

    ]]>         After 50 EU summits, leaders are still copy‑pasting failed migration ‘solutions’ https://euobserver.com/241527/after-50-eu-summits-leaders-are-still-copypasting-failed-migration-solutions/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 13:39:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241527 A trawl through 52 sets of summit conclusions reveals how EU leaders keep quietly copy‑pasting calls for tougher returns and externalised border control, while largely sidelining legal migration and resettlement schemes that could save lives.]]> EU leaders meeting next week in Brussels for the usual post-summer European Council are rehashing conclusions on migration, echoing almost word-for-word statements since at least 2015.

    “The European Council has developed a strategy aimed at stemming the unprecedented migratory flows Europe is facing,” they announced in December 2015, following a summit.

    “It is indispensable to regain control over the external borders,” they also said, noting the perceived threat to the EU’s internal border-free Schengen zone.

    And they voiced fear over the low number of deportations, insisting on “concrete measures to ensure the actual return and readmission of people not authorised to stay.”

    Eeleven years later and the 15 October summit in Brussels next week is now asking almost the same thing, including to what extent previous conclusions on migration have been implemented.

    Although draft conclusions can change, and likely will, the current wording essentially repeats the same demands spanning over 50 EU summits since at least 2015, when over a million Syrians entered Europe to seek protection.

    Out of the 52 published conclusions since 2015, over half dealt with migration in some shape or form. The latest draft dated 5 October and seen by EUobserver is among those.

    ]]>         Sanctions in February, handshakes in September: EU’s flip-flop Iran policy is putting lives at risk https://euobserver.com/241462/sanctions-in-february-handshakes-in-september-eus-flip-flop-iran-policy-is-putting-lives-at-risk/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 10:42:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241462 By sitting down with senior Iranian figures who publicly back the Revolutionary Guard while keeping sanctions limited to technocratic lists, EU governments risk undermining their own leverage at a time of rising regional tensions.]]> Why would the European Union list the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organisation in February, and then, seven months later, have its top diplomat sit down with the foreign minister of the government the Guard Corps defends?

    At the UN General Assembly last month, EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas met Abbas Araghchi, who served in the Guard Corps during the Iran–Iraq war.

    Dutch prime minister Rob Jetten met president Masoud Pezeshkian, who in 2019 joined fellow parliamentarians in wearing the Guard Corps uniform to protest Washington’s terrorist designation of it. France, Italy, and Norway held meetings of their own.

    These talks came less than nine months after Iranian security forces, on 8 and 9 January, killed protesters on a scale without precedent in the country’s modern history.

    The human rights group HRANA has verified more than 7,000 deaths, and the UN special rapporteur warned that the toll may exceed 20,000.

    In September, the UN fact-finding mission concluded that the crackdown amounted to crimes against humanity. Nor has the killing stopped: Iran Human Rights counted at least 532 executions in the first eight months of this year, including protesters arrested in January.

    After a massacre, a foreign policy guided by European values should pursue one aim above others: making a repetition more costly for those who would order and carry it out.

    Naming and shaming raises the reputational cost of repression, targeted sanctions raise its material cost, and delegitimisation raises the political cost of staying loyal to the regime.

    They work only in combination, since sanctions without delegitimization tell the regime’s elite that their assets are at risk, but their standing is not.

    Read more

    Why the Iran uprising is Europe’s strategic blind spot

    EU vs US sanctions

    Europe has used the first two instruments. The EU listed the Guard Corps in February and sanctioned additional Iranian officials for human rights abuses.

    However, these measures target assets and individuals, while the government that presided over the killing keeps its seat at the top table.

    The UNGA in New York showed how little the third instrument has been used.

    The terrorist listing freezes the Guard Corps’ funds. Neither Araghchi nor Pezeshkian is on an EU sanctions list.

    Yet it leaves a question unanswered: how far should the logic of a terrorist designation extend to the government that funds and publicly defends it?

    Article 21 of the Treaty on European Union requires the Union’s external action to be guided by human rights and to be consistent.

    Branding the Guard Corps a terrorist organisation in Brussels while posing for photographs with the government it defends in New York sits uneasily with that obligation.

    This inconsistency is costly. In a study in foreign policy analysis, my co-authors and I examined how Iranians reacted to US sanctions. Comprehensive sanctions produced a rally around the government, even among reformists.

    The 2019 designation of the Guard Corps, by contrast, produced almost no rally outside the regime’s hardliner core. Thus, targeted pressure on the security apparatus does not drive Iranians into its arms.

    Handshakes, on the other hand, may give the apparatus exactly what targeted sanctions are meant to withhold: international legitimacy.

    The photographs from New York reach two audiences.

    The first sits inside the state: an officer deciding whether to fire on a crowd, or to step aside, weighs one question above most others, namely whether the regime will survive, and each of those photographs suggests an answer.

    The second audience is the families of those killed, executed, and blinded since January. For them, the message is that Europe has moved on after eight months.

    Read more

    Reporting when the internet goes dark

    A picture is worth a thousand words

    I am not against diplomacy. Kallas raised the sharp rise in executions with Araghchi, and Jetten raised human rights and Iranian actions on Dutch soil with Pezeshkian. Channels on shipping, detained Europeans, and de-escalation should stay open.

    My objection concerns the level and the format: a meeting between leaders, photographed at the General Assembly with no public conditions attached, is not a technical channel.

    Concerns voiced in private do not travel as far as the photograph, which signals normal relations with a government that has done nothing to earn them.

    Four steps would help.

    First, the Council should agree on a common line: contact at the technical and envoy level, and leader-level meetings only on public conditions, beginning with a halt to protest-related executions.

    Second, human rights sanctions should move up the chain of command, to those who answer politically for the security forces.

    Third, member states should invest in accountability that does not depend on Tehran, such as universal jurisdiction cases and evidence-sharing with the UN mission.

    Finally, Europe should engage openly with Iran’s democratic opposition.

    The EU has already decided, in law, what the Guard Corps is. Its leaders have yet to act accordingly. A massacre answered with sanctions in February and handshakes in September does not raise the cost of the next one. It lowers it.

    ]]>         Why Oxygen Forensics US tech CEO selling software to Europe agencies was arrested https://euobserver.com/241481/why-oxygen-forensics-us-tech-ceo-selling-software-to-europe-agencies-was-arrested/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 09:59:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241481 US authorities arrested men who sold a forensic software to government bodies across Europe, hid the tool's true owners and concealed its Russian development.]]> US prosecutors say an American forensic tool concealed its Russian owners and its development in Russia.

    Used by numerous security agencies in Europe, Oxygen Forensics helps investigators worldwide access data from mobile phones and computers.

    Many bodies are now suspending use of the software following recent revelations.

    The Slovak interior ministry bought the software in 2018 when links to Russia were not yet publicly known, then renewed the license multiple times. Now, the ministry said IT department officials are investigating the issue.

    The tool was also sold to other government bodies across Europe.

    Russian ownership via Cyprus

    In the US, Virginia-based Oxygen Forensics CEO Lee Reiber was arrested at the end of September, along with Oleg Davydov, one of the Russian owners.

    The company was headquartered in the US state of Virginia, appearing American.

    According to federal prosecutors in the US, the company hid its Russian ownership through a shell company in Cyprus and that its software was developed in Russia.

    Allegedly, this scam helped secure contracts for the forensic tool in the US, UK, Czech Republic, Latvia, Romania, and Slovakia.

    Reiber, a 55-year-old American, was arrested in Idaho on Sunday. On Tuesday (22 September), he appeared before a federal court there and was released on bail. He is expected to appear before a federal court in Los Angeles soon.

    Davydov, a 52-year-old from Moscow, was arrested on that same day at London Heathrow before he could board a flight to Istanbul. And the US plans to seek extradition. Both face charges of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

    The group of five also owned a Russian company co-founded by Davydov in 2000. Until September 2022, it was called Oxygen Software and now operates under the name MKO Systems.

    Its programmers worked in Russia, where the company sold the software under other names. According to investigative files, its clients included Russia’s secret service (FSB), investigative committee (SKR) and interior ministry.

    Read more

    Shadow fleet tankers flock back to being flagged as Russian, creating more headaches for EU states

    Davydov, the company’s technical director, was responsible for software development. In 2013, he helped establish Oxygen Forensics in Virginia with Reiber joining the company in August 2015.

    Prosecutors say that following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and US sanctions after, the duo agreed to hide both the real owners and that it was developed in Russia. In March 2022, Reiber became CEO and director.

    Then, Russian owners were removed from public company records.

    However, investigators said the Russians continued to control the company, making key decisions, determining Reiber’s pay, and outvoting him on the board.

    The charges concern the concealment of the software’s ownership and origin in securing public contracts.

    A network of deception

    Two companies were found to have supplied the Slovak interior ministry with Oxygen Forensic tools.

    In 2018, the sale was part of a broader procurement by the ministry for computers, laptops, servers, monitors and printers, ordered from the Czech company Risk Analysis Consultants for €125,000, the forensic tool itself costing €10,000.

    The Prague-based company did not respond for comment.

    An invoice issued to the Slovak interior ministry in 2022 by the Slovak company Microcomp–Computersystém indicates the renewal of a licence for this software. At the time, the minister responsible was Roman Mikulec.

    The Slovak ministry also ordered a licence renewal in July 2024, under his successor Matúš Šutaj Eštok. Microcomp–Computersystém did not respond for comment.

    Authorities warned

    On Friday (2 October), the Slovak national security authority (NBÚ) warned of the risks posed by using software from Oxygen Forensics and connected companies such as MKO Systems and Prostranstvo IT.

    Their software helps investigators search for and examine data from digital devices. It can process vast amounts of information, including evidence, which makes it important who owns, controls and develops it. According to the NBÚ, this is important both for data protection and for the reliability of analysis results.

    The warning came after the US case was made public.

    The NBÚ considers links to Russia significant in assessing the security risk, also in view of Russia’s military aggression against Ukraine.

    However, the warning itself does not mean that data leaked through the software. US prosecutors explicitly stated that the charges did not concern malicious code or unauthorised access to customer data.

    The case concerns the alleged concealment of the software’s ownership and origin. And no court has yet ruled on the case.

    “The ministry will proceed in accordance with the recommendations of the National Security Authority,” the Slovak interior ministry said.

    The NBÚ recommended that public bodies identify this company’s presence and report it to the authority.

    Belgian Green MEP Saskia Bricmont also called for the use of Oxygen to be stopped immediately and for an inquiry into whether sensitive information could have reached Russia after it was found that Romania, Germany, Spain, Italy, Poland and Hungary had purchased the software.

    Read more

    German ex-spy chief arrested over espionage and treason allegations involving leaked BND files

    European police shed tool

    Several European security agencies are suspending the use of Oxygen Forensics software or taking steps to terminate their contracts after the company’s Russian ties came to light.

    The tool was also used by Czech police. Czech security agencies continued to purchase licences for the computer software after 2022, when the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Czech authorities are awaiting further information from the United States. For now, they have prohibited software updates.

    London’s Metropolitan Police has suspended the use of Oxygen tools and launched a comprehensive review. British police forces, including specialised units, had used the software.

    And Latvian police suspended its use and is assessing whether it will continue using it.

    Romania’s anti-corruption agency, too, took steps to terminate its contract with the Russia-linked tool.

    ]]>         EU will need to tax AI ‘workers’ to keep funding human pensions https://euobserver.com/241372/eu-will-need-to-tax-ai-workers-to-keep-funding-human-pensions/ Wed, 07 Oct 2026 08:50:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241372 As AI shifts work from people to machines, it will force a rethink of who gets taxed, on what, and where. Nowhere is that question more urgent than in Europe, which funds the world's most comprehensive welfare states primarily through taxes on work.]]> Every major technological shift reshapes not just the economy but the tax system that pays for it. When big corporations emerged, corporate and payroll taxes followed. When mass car ownership took hold, fuel duties emerged to pay for the roads it required. 

    As AI shifts work from people to machines, it will force a rethink of who gets taxed, on what, and where. Nowhere is that question more urgent than in Europe, which funds the world’s most comprehensive welfare states primarily through taxes on work.

    Taxes on work make up 51.5 percent of all tax revenue in the EU-27, according to the European Commission’s latest Taxation Trends data — a share that rose in 2024. These charges are taken straight from the payslip. They’re hard to avoid, and scale with employment.

    AI, by replacing human work with software and machines, eats away at exactly this tax base. 

    The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates that around 40 percent of jobs worldwide are exposed to AI. If that leads to fewer workers, it will also mean fewer payslips, pension contributions and social charges, weakening the revenue streams that fund Europe’s pension and healthcare systems. This is not a distant problem; the costs are already mounting.

    Read more

    EU not ‘lagging’ US in AI-productivity gains, Lagarde tells MEPs

    Shift the burden to corporate profits

    The obvious response is to shift more of the tax burden onto corporate profits, which will increasingly reflect the gains firms make by deploying AI instead of hiring workers.

    Unlike a tax on machines and equipment themselves, a profit tax falls mostly on excess profits and need not distort investment. The case for shifting weight from payroll taxes to profits is strong and strengthens as AI replaces more workers with machines.

    But profits, unlike payrolls, move. A company can locate its intellectual property in a low-rate jurisdiction — a pattern Europe knows well from decades of profits routed through Ireland and Luxembourg — and ensure that profits are booked far from where the jobs are lost. It is how the world’s largest technology and AI firms already operate.

    Read more

    Reverse centaurs: EU approach to AI risks dystopia for human workers

    Two-pillar answer

    The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD’s) Inclusive Framework was designed to address exactly this: profits shifted across jurisdictions to avoid tax, and e-commerce allowed sales where firms have no physical presence. AI makes these reforms more urgent. 

    Pillar One of the framework put forward by the Paris-based wealthy nations’ club addresses where a corporation is taxed. It shifts partial taxing rights for the largest multinationals away from where they are headquartered and toward where their customers and users are located. 

    Still under negotiation, it would apply only to a handful of the largest firms, but many AI companies would qualify. 

    These firms are concentrated in a select number of countries, very few of them European, but the displacement they cause, and the public services that displaced workers will require, will weigh heavily on European budgets.

    Pillar Two of the OECD framework introduces a global minimum corporate tax of 15 percent on multinationals with revenues above €750m.

    The EU moved first and furthest: Council Directive (EU) 2022/2523 made the minimum tax binding across the Union from 2024, and 22 of the 27 member states now apply it in full. The United States, notably, has not implemented the rules. 

    Read more

    Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

    Politics is undermining the fix

    But the obstacles are real. US ratification of the OECD proposals is unlikely, and many of the largest companies are headquartered there. 

    The pressure is already reshaping Europe’s own rules: under the G7’s June 2025 ‘side-by-side’ agreement, US-parented groups would be exempt from the EU’s minimum-tax rules: a carveout the European Commission confirmed in January 2026 and which several member states consider legally fragile. 

    The Commission also dropped its proposed EU digital levy under US trade pressure, leaving a patchwork of national digital services taxes in France, Italy, Spain, Austria, and elsewhere.

    Such exceptions and carveouts show that big-power politics can hollow out the framework. These reforms were designed to address the tax challenges for an AI-economy. They were good policy then. They are fiscal necessities now. Fairer corporate taxation will not be enough, but it is a start. 

    Europe’s choice

    The EU has instruments on the table, the BEFIT common corporate tax base and the proposed Corporate Resource for Europe, but both remain politically contested.

    European governments that fail to act will be managing the social costs of technological disruption with a tax system built for the industrial age, while the profits that fund their rivals accumulate beyond their reach.

    Even if Europeans work less, their needs for health care, pensions, and consumption remain. As wage-based contributions shrink, Europe must shift more of the tax burden onto corporate profits and close off the routes that let those profits move beyond the reach of the states bearing the costs of automation. 

    Productivity gains may soften the arithmetic; they will not repeal it. The tax base must follow the economy.

      <title>Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing</link>
      <description><p>Lawyer for CNN, MS Now and Politico says Trump admitted he banned networks from White House over their coverage</p><p>Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.</p><p>The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/08/trump-media-ban-hearing">Continue reading...</a></description>

    <item>
      <title>Millionaire tax no more? Rightwing groups lead effort to repeal Washington state law</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax</link>
      <description><p>An initiative on November’s ballot aims to overturn the 9.9% tax on earnings above $1m – who’s winning the fight? </p><p>Voters in Washington state will soon decide the fate of the state’s so-called “<a href="https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/millionaires-tax-faq/">millionaire tax</a>” – a 9.9% income tax on earnings above $1m that was <a href="https://governor.wa.gov/news/2026/governor-ferguson-signs-millionaires-tax-law">signed</a> into law in March and is now facing a conservative-backed effort to repeal it.</p><p>An <a href="https://leg.wa.gov/media/ucubvqsd/2026-summary-of-initiative-26-645.pdf">initiative</a> on November’s ballot aims to overturn the tax, claiming that the tax represents a slippery slope, and would eventually result in taxes for more than just millionaires. A <a href="https://no645.com/our-coalition/">coalition</a> of advocacy groups and unions opposing the initiative say taxing the state’s 20,000 highest-earning households could raise approximately $3.5bn in necessary annual revenue to fund core priorities like education and healthcare, and expand tax credits and sales tax exemptions.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/07/washington-state-millionaire-tax">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 08 Oct 2026 22:20:13 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Jim O’Callaghan dismisses claims of Garda ‘resignation crisis’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/ocallaghan-dismisses-claims-of-garda-resignation-crisis/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/08/ocallaghan-dismisses-claims-of-garda-resignation-crisis/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 18:56:06 +0000The strength of the Garda force is about to reach record levels, despite claims for years from the Garda Representative Association (GRA) that resignations and retirements are at crisis levels, Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan has said.

He has also dismissed suggestions the expected all-time peak in Garda numbers, from 14,500 at present to 15,000 in the coming months, will prove very brief and will be almost immediately followed by a surge in age-related retirements that could continue for about a decade.

During that period, according to the Garda’s own projections, the number of gardaí who will reach compulsory retirement age in any one year is set to increase 10-fold.

The GRA, which represents more than 11,000 rank and file gardaí, said while there was provision made in the budget for recruiting up to 1,000 additional gardaí next year, in the first nine months of this year some 400 members had retired or resigned. But O’Callaghan has insisted recruitment is far ahead of retirements or resignations.

“The number of resignations from An Garda Síochána is extraordinarily low, if you look at the PSNI, or any of the police forces in the UK,” O’Callaghan said in a budget event in Dublin on Thursday, insisting that, despite claims to the contrary, the Garda force does not have a resignations problem.

“(Garda resignations) are at about 1 per cent, 140 resignations a year. And, talking to the Garda Commissioner, he tells me that many people who resign come back, and they can be fast-tracked back in.”

He added Garda recruitment was “going well”, with classes of 200 or more now passing out regularly at the Garda College, Templemore, Co Tipperary, and he hoped there could be five such passing out ceremonies per year.

“It’s a great job and a lot of people now realise they want to do a job that doesn’t involve sending and receiving emails all day. And if you become a garda, you’re not doing that,” he said.

Garda retirements set to surge in ‘ticking time-bomb’, projections show

O’Callaghan added retirements from the Garda were “inevitable”. However, he regularly approved extensions of service for members who had reached 62 years, the compulsory age of retirement, but had applied for special permission to continue working for an extra one or two years.

GRA general secretary Ronan Slevin said successive governments had made the same budget promises to increase the Garda by 1,000 members the following year, with minimal impact.

“We presented the Government with a six-point plan suggesting how we could solve a recruitment and retention crisis but have been ignored,” he said.

“We are now on the eve of national pay talks and we still haven’t been told if we will even be in the room when our financial futures are being shaped.

“As of this week, almost 400 gardaí have left the job in 2026 through resignations and retirements, and this number will only get higher by the end of the year.

“The sheer lack of direct engagement by Minister Chambers and his department with the elected members of the GRA has been, for us, disappointing, disingenuous and almost disrespectful.”

The retirement age for Garda members was last year increased from 60 to 62. This had the effect of postponing the start of a projected decade-long retirement spike.

Some gardaí working until age 64 for the first time in history of force

For example, the latest projections by Garda Headquarters show that next year and the year after, the number of Garda members who will reach compulsory retirement age is 37 and 49. However, that is then set to increase every year, for the next decade and will reach 373 by 2035, a ten-fold increase.

Furthermore, the retirement spike will probably start sooner, and worsen more quickly than Garda Headquarters’ projections. This is because the projections are based on all Garda members continuing to work until they are aged 62 years.

In reality, many serving members have a full pension once they reach 30 years service and can retire at any point after they reach the age of 50 years.

]]>Enda O Dowd <![CDATA[Galway bar manager dismissed just 11 days after miscarriage awarded €25,000]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/08/bar-manager-let-go-after-miscarriage-awarded-25000/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/08/bar-manager-let-go-after-miscarriage-awarded-25000/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:05:54 +0000A Galway hospitality firm which dismissed a manager just 11 days after she suffered a miscarriage, before trying to claim that maternity protection law didn’t apply since she wasn’t pregnant any longer, has been ordered to pay her €25,000.

Fadeside Ltd, a subsidiary of the Connacht Hospitality Group, has been ordered by the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) to compensate a former manager at its Residence Hotel and 1520 Bar in Galway City for terminating her employment in October 2023 on the stated basis of underperformance.

It is said to be the first time a worker has sought to have the minimum service requirements of the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 set aside under maternity protection law in the circumstances of a miscarriage.

Normally, an employee requires 12 months’ service before they can pursue a complaint for unfair dismissal – a limitation disapplied in relation to pregnant workers, who are shielded from day one.

The complainant fell ill and was admitted to A&E in September 2023. She found out then that she had been pregnant and was having a miscarriage, she said in evidence to the tribunal.

At the time, she was just under 11 months into a new €60,000-a-year job as general manager at the hotel and bar in Galway’s Latin Quarter.

She said that, after phoning in sick, group HR manager Jackie O’Dowd reached her by phone and said the miscarriage “would make [the complainant] want to have a baby even more”.

At the WRC, O’Dowd denied making the remark.

The complainant said she told O’Dowd in reply that getting pregnant was not something she had planned.

Having returned to work in the first week of October 2023, the worker met her line manager, Wayne Neilon, later telling the WRC she wanted to discuss her working hours and other business maters, she said.

The complainant said Neilon told her she “did not have the core competencies” for the job.

O’Dowd then arrived and asked whether the complainant wanted to resign, remarking that perhaps she “needed a break” because of the miscarriage, the complainant said.

She was told at the meeting that her probation would not be extended and received a letter of dismissal citing “work performance” the following day, the tribunal was told.

The complainant said Neilon had told her months earlier, in May 2023, that she had passed her probation, and that she said so at the October meeting.

In any case, the WRC noted the complainant’s contract capped the maximum probation period at 11 months; by the time of the October meeting, she had 11 months and two days’ service.

The firm’s solicitor, Pat Mullins of O’Flynn Exhams LLP, failed in March of last year in an attempt to have the case thrown out, arguing that enhanced workplace protections under the Maternity Protection Act did not extend to the complainant.

“At the time of the dismissal, the complainant was not, in fact, pregnant, and I say it is a substantial stretch of the interpretation of that part of the Act to state that it includes a previous miscarriage,” Mullins said.

Counsel for the worker, Ian FitzHarris, with Orlaith J Byrne & Co solicitors, said the sacking was just 11 days after the pregnancy loss, his client having worked just five more days after her absence, he said.

“Five days and then they sacked her. The phrase in the legislation is ‘pregnancy-related matters’,” counsel said.

Adjudicator Louise Boyle rejected the respondent’s stance on maternity rights. “It is not in dispute that a miscarriage arises from pregnancy,” she wrote.

“I find that in all the circumstances it lacks credibility that the complainant’s employment was terminated for poor performance,” she wrote.

She concluded the respondent had failed to demonstrate there were the “exceptional circumstances” required to dismiss a worker entitled to maternity protections and awarded €25,000 for unfair dismissal.

]]>urbazon<![CDATA[Global shares fall as oil tops $105 amid fresh tanker attacks by Iran]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/shares-fall-as-middle-east-tanker-attacks-drive-oil-prices-higher/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/08/shares-fall-as-middle-east-tanker-attacks-drive-oil-prices-higher/Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:34:30 +0000Global shares fell on Thursday as oil topped $105 amid fresh tanker attacks by Iran, which threaten to curtail a recent uptick in flows from the Middle East and adding to worries over rising inflation globally.

Risk assets took a hit, while a sell-off in bank stocks that started in Asia fed into other markets. Meanwhile, the bond market rout showed no sign of abating as US and French yields continued to rise.

DUBLIN

The Iseq index underperformed its peers, falling by more than 2 per cent. Ireland’s pillar banks were caught up in a global sell-off of lenders, with AIB, down by 3.6 per cent to €10.90, the worst performer on the index.

Bank of Ireland shed 2.5 per cent to close at €18.43. The Irish Times reported on Thursday that the lender has managed to contain losses in its US leveraged acquisition loan book through insurance deals with specialist investors.

Ryanair fell by 2.5 per cent to €23.37 per share after Michael O’Leary warned that “insanely higher” jet fuel prices could last until 2028.

All of the big names on the index finished in red, including Kerry Group, down by 0.4 per cent, and Kingspan, which slid by 0.7 per cent.

LONDON

British shares dipped, with the benchmark FTSE 100 falling by 0.2 per cent and the mid-cap FTSE 250 shedding almost 0.5 per cent.

The big names in British banking faltered. Lloyds gave back almost 1.7 per cent amid renewed attacks on tankers in the Gulf. HSBC shed almost 2 per cent after the FT reported that the bank plans deep job cuts in its ‌UK wealth business ⁠as part of a broader, AI-driven efficiency push.

Among individual stocks, Tesco surged by more than 5 per cent after the food retailer raised its profit forecast.

Asset management company ‌Aberdeen rose 1.4 per cent after selling 52 million ​shares in Standard Life for about £436 million.

EUROPE

Europe’s main equity indices were dragged lower by falling bank stocks. The blue-chip Stoxx 50 was down by almost 1 per cent and the pan-European Stoxx 600 dipped by 0.7 per cent ata nearly four-month low.

European lenders have this week suffered their worst two-day slump since March amid concerns over France’s fiscal deficit and political gridlock.

Italy’s Intesa Sanpaolo shed almost 3 per cent as Spain’s BBVA and Santander fell by 1.8 per cent and 2.9 per cent, respectively.

France’s BNP Paribas fell by 2.4 per cent, while its compatriot, Société Générale, dipped 2.3 per cent.

Among individual stocks, Argenx tumbled by almost 16 per cent, making it the worst performer on the Stoxx 600, after the Netherlands-based biopharmaceutical ​company discontinued a trial.

Most sectors on the STOXX traded lower. Energy shares were a bright spot as oil prices climbed more than 3 per cent on persistent concerns about supply from the ‌key Middle East producing region.

NEW YORK

US stocks fell as a surge in oil prices and treasury yields ‌near multiyear highs stoked inflation worries before a crucial earnings season that is expected to test recent market gains.

Megacap growth stocks were broadly lower, ​with Amazon falling by around 1 per cent and Tesla down 1.4 per cent.

Chip-related companies also dropped after forecasts of record quarterly profit from memory-chip giant Samsung Electronics failed to lift sentiment, with its shares closing ⁠lower in South Korea.

Rival Micron Technology was down 1.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Broadcom is lining up $50 ‌billion ‌in ​financing for OpenAI, with Oracle also seeking an unspecified sum, spurring fears that large debt issuance by technology companies could intensify the competition for capital.

Broadcom and Oracle were down 1.4 per cent and 2.1 per cent, respectively, amid wider weakness in ⁠tech stocks. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg, Reuters
