One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate.

Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives.

The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content.

W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5

— Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026

The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning.

A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised.

The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily.

The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.

The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.

Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.

The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.

At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).

After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.

In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).

And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).

Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, thanked both Sweden and the Netherlands for their role in defending Polish airspace and NATO’s eastern flank.

“The continuity of this mission is an expression of allied solidarity and shared responsibility for the region’s security in the face of the threat from Russia. Together we are stronger,” he wrote on social media.

His deputy minister, Paweł Zalewski, told broadcaster TVN that Patriot systems “are currently the only ones effective against ballistic missiles”, making them vital for protecting Rzeszów. He noted that around 90% of international aid for Ukraine goes through the hub.

Poland has also been taking delivery of its own Patriot systems from the United States. The first were deployed at Warsaw Babice airport in 2023. Last year, Poland announced full operational readiness of its US-supplied Integrated Battle Command System (IBCS), an air-defence network that includes Patriot missile batteries.

Dziękuję rządowi Szwecji za podjęcie decyzji o wysłaniu do Polski systemów Patriot. Szwedzi przejmą ochronę hubu logistycznego NATO w Rzeszowie.
Dziękuję także Holandii 🇳🇱 za dotychczasowe wsparcie Polski i wschodniej flanki NATO. Ciągłość tej misji to wyraz sojuszniczej…

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 6, 2026

Earlier this year, Poland’s airspace was violated by a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, which landed in a field. On one night last year, around 20 Russian drones crossed the country’s eastern borders, and last month a Russian military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.

The growing threat from Russia has pushed Poland to forge closer military ties with other countries around the Baltic Sea, and above all with Sweden. In 2024, the two countries signed a strategic partnership to enhance cooperation on defence and economic development.

Since then, they have held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic; Poland has ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab; and Sweden bought €274 million worth of Piorun man-portable air-defence systems from Polish firm Mesko.

Poland has detained and charged five current and former senior managers at state energy giant Orlen as part of an investigation into allegations that the company artificially lowered fuel prices in the run-up to the 2023 parliamentary election.

At the time, many experts and the then-opposition – which won that election and is now in power – accused Orlen of cutting prices to help the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party’s re-election campaign.

Prosecutors say that the decisions made by the executives constituted “a gross violation of procedures” and caused “over 4.1 billion zloty” (€938 million) of financial damage to the company. If found guilty, the accused could face up to 25 years in prison.

Prokurator przedstawił pięciu menadżerom Orlen S.A. zarzuty wyrządzenia spółce szkody w wysokości ponad 4,1 mld zł w związku z nierynkowym kształtowaniem cen paliw w 2023 r. ⬇️https://t.co/yjiaX0ehHu

— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) October 6, 2026

At the end of August 2023, just over a month before the elections, Orlen, which controls around 60% of Poland’s fuel market, began sharply cutting its wholesale petrol prices as well as the prices at the large network of petrol stations it runs.

By early October, the wholesale price of unleaded petrol had fallen by nearly 12.7%, while average prices at petrol stations had dropped by about 10%.

The price cuts, however, puzzled experts because oil prices on international markets were rising and the zloty was weakening, both of which would normally push fuel prices higher.

The relatively low prices in Poland encouraged some motorists from neighbouring countries to travel to Poland to tank up, while some Polish drivers began stockpiling fuel. Just days after the election, held on 15 October, fuel prices began to rise.

State oil firm Orlen's wholesale petrol prices have risen this week after falling in the leadup to Sunday’s elections

Some had accused Orlen of artificially lowering prices to help the ruling party’s election campaign and warned they would rise afterwards https://t.co/FLUs1n8EA9

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 19, 2023

Figures from the then-opposition accused Orlen of lowering prices to win popularity for the government ahead of the elections. Under the leadership of its then-CEO, Daniel Obajtek, the company had regularly carried out actions seen as beneficial for the ruling PiS party. Obajtek is now a PiS MEP.

In October 2023, Krzysztof Brejza, a lawmaker from the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then in opposition and is now Poland’s main ruling party – notified prosecutors of a potential crime. He claimed that strategic fuel reserves had been emptied as part of Orlen’s price-cutting move.

Now, after a lengthy investigation, prosecutors have announced that five current and former managers have been detained. One, named only as Michał R. under Polish privacy law, served as a member of Orlen’s board from 2018 to 2024.

The others are identified as an executive director, two office directors, and the head of a department responsible for pricing.

 

The National Prosecutor’s Office said that all five had been charged with causing large-scale economic damage, which carries a prison sentence of between five and 25 years.

“The charges concern abuse of power and failure to fulfil managerial duties, causing damage to Orlen in the amount of over 4.1 billion złoty in connection with the implemented pricing policy,” wrote prosecutors.

They said that the main aim of that pricing policy was to keep the price of fuels below the psychological threshold of 6 zloty per litre, and that this was carried out “in a manner detached from market realities…in gross violation of numerous formal and informal procedures applicable to the managerial staff at Orlen”.

Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new @FT report on how state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million through a botched effort to buy Venezuelan oil under the former government https://t.co/LlGcgXOvGG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026

Speaking anonymously to broadcaster TVN, one of the prosecutors involved in the case said that the executives’ actions had implications not only for Orlen’s finances, but also Poland’s national security, given that strategic reserves are meant to be saved for emergency situation.

“State security was jeopardised for the sake of politics,” they said. “These reserves are intended, at a time of war, to ensure there is fuel for tanks, to put it simply.”

Meanwhile, justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, wrote on social media that Orlen and Obajtek had, by “manually controlling prices”, “acted to the detriment of national assets in order to save the party’s [grip on] power”.

Na polecenie łódzkiego wydziału ds. Przestępczości Zorganizowanej Prokuratury Krajowej funkcjonariusze ABW zatrzymali wczoraj 5 byłych i obecnych menadżerów Orlen S.A., w tym byłego członka zarządu spółki z lat 2018-2024.

Jesienią 2023 roku Daniel „wszystko mogę” Obajtek ręcznie… https://t.co/qV9qroeBu0

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 6, 2026

Obajtek today rejected the allegations and defended Orlen’s actions under his leadership. He accused the current government of acting to distract from its own failure to keep fuel prices under control.

“They couldn’t cope with rising fuel prices so – for show and without any substantive justification – they’re detaining experienced managers thanks to whom fuel cost less than 6 zloty [per litre] in the summer and autumn of 2023,” he wrote on social media.

“If I have to answer for the fact that Poles paid little for fuel, then I would be honoured,” he added.

However, speaking at a press conference, Żurek declared that, “in a state governed by law there are proper procedures for lowering prices”. Instead, under PiS, there was “a state of lawlessness, a state run like a private fiefdom”.

Nie potrafili poradzić sobie z rosnącymi cenami paliw, więc – na pokaz, bez żadnego merytorycznego uzasadnienia – zatrzymują doświadczonych managerów, dzięki którym paliwo latem i jesienią 2023 roku kosztowało poniżej 6 złotych, gdy baryłka ropy była po 100 dolarów, a dolar 4,20…

— Daniel Obajtek (@DanielObajtek) October 5, 2026

In a separate case, the European Parliament last year stripped Obajtek of legal immunity to face charges for allegedly using Orlen’s funds to serve his own private interests. Polish prosecutors are also pursuing him for allegedly violating Poland’s press law and falsely reporting his income in a tax return.

Last month, the Financial Times reported on how, under Obajtek’s leadership, Orlen lost $230 million (856 million zloty) trying to buy Venezuelan oil through intermediaries, unsecured payments and cryptocurrency transfers.

Obajtek, however, argued that he managed to turn Orlen into one of Europe’s largest companies, including diversifying it away from its traditional focus on oil and towards other forms of energy, including gas, hydrogen and renewables.

Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression.

On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus.

“In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing.

“As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added.

The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members.

Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland.

 

Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise.

This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation.

Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country.

Almost 80% of Poles say they would want Poland to come to the aid of the Baltic states if they were attacked by Russia

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 10, 2026

The two ministers also used their meeting to discuss their joint response to illegal migration. Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia.

In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027.

“Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. But for now, we have decided that they will remain in place for at least another six months.”

Poland is reintroducing controls on its borders with Germany and Lithuania to prevent the “uncontrolled flow of migrants”, in particular those returned by Germany after entering illegally

"Poland’s patience is running out," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/Pttd3FvpHA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2025

Katelynas emphasised that “Lithuania and Poland share a common goal: to ensure the protection of our borders and effectively prevent irregular migrants from moving through our countries and across the Schengen area”.

He also noted that an agreement between the two countries on cooperation between police, border guard and customs services is currently being finalised.

“Poland and Lithuania are like brothers and sisters who support each other and will continue to do so,” said Katelynas.

Kierwiński likewise expressed his satisfaction that the two countries “speak with one voice…because this part of Europe, the eastern flank of NATO and the EU, must speak with one voice to address and counter the threats posed by Russian imperialism and the difficult situation beyond our eastern border”.

She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025

Last month, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental.

Poland has already recently suffered airspace violations by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter. It has also been the primary target for Russian sabotage operations in Europe.

In response, the Polish government has moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters.

The Polish-Lithuanian border area, which sits between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and is known as the Suwałki Gap, is seen as a potential target for Russia in the event of war. ]]> Reports claim Trump tried to change Poland’s government. What do we know? https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/05/reports-claim-trump-tried-to-change-polands-government-what-do-we-know/ Mon, 05 Oct 2026 18:22:20 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105036

Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition.

Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”.

Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”.

Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue.

The context

Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners.

One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister.

Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election.

By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner.

The meeting

The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way.

On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”.

The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki.

In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”.

Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so.

 

The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan.

“I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation.

What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz?

Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Tusk and form a new government with the right-wing opposition.

“Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk.

She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski.

Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”.

What has Poland’s government said?

On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base.

“In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?”

Z tak ważnej rozmowy organizator miał obowiązek sporządzić notatkę. Do @MSZ_RP ona nie dotarła.
Czyżby dlatego, że spotkanie służyło też próbie zaangażowania obcego państwa w naszą wewnętrzną politykę? https://t.co/0wL0QZBxPv

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 2, 2026

On Monday, Tusk himself told broadcaster TVN that Kosiniak-Kamysz had informed him about his meeting with Trump immediately after it took place. He added that the subject of the meeting “is too interesting to talk about publicly”, but that military “bases were not the topic of the conversation”.

“The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk.

Kosiniak-Kamysz himself also confirmed on Monday that the question of a permanent US base in Poland had not been discussed at the meeting. He noted that, in March, that issue was not even seriously on the table, because it was only two months later that Trump announced he intended to send additional troops to Poland

The defence minister did not give any further details about the content of the meeting, which he described as “informal”.

Duncan Jones returns to form with a brisk, earnest Rogue Trooper, powered by strong voice work and pulp sci-fi zeal—see why it wins over.]]>

Rogue Trooper | Dir. Duncan Jones | ★★★★☆

Duncan Jones exploded onto the film scene in 2009 with his debut Moon, an elegiac sci-fi thriller about a sad astronaut (Sam Rockwell) grappling with an existential crisis. Since then Jones’ rockets have failed to ignite in such spectacular fashion: Source Code starring Jake Gyllenhaal was a smart if somewhat forgettable blockbuster; video game adaptation Warcraft was a disaster; and the less said about 2018’s Mute, an overblown homage to Blade Runner, the better.

But Jones is not a man who is easily deterred and science fiction clearly runs through his very veins. His latest project is an adaptation of Rogue Trooper from the cult-classic British anthology comic 2000 AD (best known as the home of Judge Dredd), rendered in computer animation that is stylistically not a million miles away from Warcraft, albeit without the live action elements. 

If you’re wondering who let Jones loose with the mega-budget required for yet another feature-length animation (Warcraft cost a reported $160m), the answer is… nobody, really. Rogue Trooper was made on a decidedly indie-movie budget of between $10m and $20m, utilising video game creation tool Unreal Engine 5 for its production. 

The result is a lovingly crafted if strangely earnest love letter to pulp science fiction, old-school war movies and video games. 

Rogue Trooper: A video game come to life

The first thing you notice, in fact, is just how much Rogue Trooper looks like a video game. The animation style will be immediately familiar to anyone who’s picked up a controller in the last ten years or so; the whole project has the air of a cut-scene from Gears of War or Cyberpunk 2077 or any number of big budget titles. It doesn’t look bad, exactly, but it shares the same… glossiness, the light reflecting in a way your brain identifies on an instinctual level as ever-so-slightly wrong, as if everything in this world is slightly clammy.

Perhaps everything in this world is slightly clammy: Rogue Trooper is set on Nu-Earth, a toxic planet-wide warzone where the fighting never stops. The Southers are making a big push against their bitter rivals the Norts, using platoons of genetically enhanced super soldiers to gain what might be a winning advantage. As well as being Captain America-style killing machines, these soldiers are also able to transfer their consciousness onto microchips should they perish in battle, allowing them to die for their country not just once but countless times. The perfect soldiers.

And so we meet 19 and his squad of blue-skinned warriors, although for most of the film 19 is the only one who still has a body: as his comrades fall, he inserts their microchips into whatever comes to hand: namely a gun, a helmet and a backpack. 

The first half of the film is essentially one long action sequence, which only serves to underscore the similarities with a video game cut-scene. The soldiers take out a fortress-sized tank, abseiling away as the thing explodes. Or they have a firefight amid a field of hallucinogenic gas, performing stealth take-downs while silhouetted against a dramatic psychedelic backdrop. There are even frequent shots of characters aiming through the scopes of their rifles, which can make Rogue Trooper feel a bit like watching a stream of Destiny or Overwatch. 

A brilliant voice acting cast

Its real strength, however, lies not in its action but in its voice acting. Aneurin Barnard is wonderfully likeable as the lead, his dulcet Welsh tones always a joy to hear amid the clamour of war, as are his band of regionally-accented brothers. It also boasts an embarrassment of talent in the supporting cast, including Matt Berry (brilliant as always), Reece Shearsmith, Diane Morgan (slightly wasted), Jemaine Clement and Sean Bean. 

Berry and Clement are especially great as two oily scavengers profiting from the destruction, but the dialogue is excellently written and delivered throughout. By the second half, you’re really invested in these characters, even the one who’s just a talking helmet.

It quite possibly makes you care about them a little too much – the Rogue Trooper of 2000 AD is a biting satire of imperialism, bureaucracy and the military-industrial complex, yet much of that satire takes a back seat to a more traditional hero’s journey.

Still, this is the best movie Jones has made since Source Code, possibly since Moon: it’s briskly entertaining from start to finish and infused with such breathless adoration for science fiction that it’s hard not to be won over.

Businesses could face a “raft” of “trivial” data protection claims if the Supreme Court rules compensation can be won for emotional distress or anxiety caused by data breaches without needing to prove any harm actually occurred, in a hearing set to conclude on Thursday.

The case was originally brought by 432 current and former police officers from the Sussex Police Force against the force’s pensions administrator, financial outsourcing firm Paymaster, following a data protection breach in 2019.

The police cohort brought the claim to recover financial compensation for non-material damage – such as distress or anxiety – over the misuse of their data in the breach which saw Paymaster mistakenly mail annual pension benefits statements containing sensitive data including names, national insurance numbers, and salaries, of approximately 450 current and former police officers to out-of-date addresses.

The Supreme Court has been asked to decide whether or not there is a threshold of seriousness in data privacy claims that can be measured. The Court of Appeal previously said there is none, but Paymaster, trading under its parent company, Equiniti, is challenging that.

In 2024, High Court Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed most of the claims and ruled that claimants had to prove the pensions statement was opened and read by a third-party. However, in 2025 the Court of Appeal overturned the decision, ruling that sending data to the wrong address can be grounds for a claim without needing proof it was read by a third party.

The court had ruled there is no minimum so-called ‘threshold of seriousness’ for data protection claims under the UK’s data protection law, the GDPR.

Claims ‘are a drain on business time and money’

If the Supreme Court refuses Paymaster’s appeal, businesses could feel the fallout.

“On the defence side, everyone is hoping that the Supreme Court reinstates some control over trivial data protection claims. Currently such claims are a drain on business time and money and claimant firms continue to pursue them. Add to that the Court system’s challenges and finite resources, then greater clarity and control will help a lot,” James Hyde, commercial disputes partner at Addleshaw Goddard told City AM.

“If it doesn’t take the opportunity, then the Court system and business will continue to be inundated by a raft of individual and group claims based on trivial and spurious grounds,” Hyde said.

As well as administering pension schemes for public sector organisations including the police, the civil service, and the Armed Forces, Equiniti also handles shareholder services and employee stock plans for roughly half of the FTSE 100 companies including Barclays, Associated British Foods, and National Grid.

Tom Moore, disputes resolution lawyer at Bird & Bird told City AM if the appeal is refused, “we are likely to see more claims brought or threatened against businesses by data subjects”, and firms will “find that any claim, no matter how trivial, can go to court without being struck out” on the basis of seriousness alone.

This comes in the same week it was revealed Goldman Sachs and Man Group’s corporate data was exposed in a data breach at Big Four giant EY earlier this year, and retailer Asos was struck by a group of hackers who duped an employee by posing as a “trusted” contact.

Sussex Police declined to comment. Equiniti was contacted for comment.

Big Four giant EY’s global revenue has hit $57bn (£43bn), up nearly 5 per cent on the previous financial year.

EY-Parthenon’s strategy arm led the firm’s overall growth across all services lines, with a 7 per cent increase. Tax grew by 6 per cent, consulting by over 4 per cent, and assurance by 3 per cent.

The Big Four stalwart said sales from AI services skyrocketed over the financial year by nearly 50 per cent due to client demand.

The firm said it invested $448m over 2026 in training and development, with a focus on AI. 

Commenting on the result, Janet Truncale, EY global chair and chief executive, said: “Growth in demand for AI-related services reflects that shift, as organisations increasingly prioritise approaches that combine technology with deep industry knowledge, trusted relationships and human judgement.”

“This fiscal year’s results demonstrate the strength of bringing EY teams and alliance partners together to accelerate value creation and turn disruption into sustained growth,” she added.

Earlier this year, EY had to withdraw a study it had produced on loyalty rewards programmes after a probe revealed it contained a string of AI hallucinations and fake footnotes.

EY’s gap with Deloitte

Last month, competitor Deloitte, reported a rise in its global revenue, hitting $74.5bn (£56.37bn).

This increase came despite its technology and transformation division slipping lower, as the consultancy sector comes under pressure from AI. 

Elsewhere in the UK, in the results we have so far, PwC’s UK revenue grew to £4.365bn, up two per cent on the previous year.

While Deloitte UK revenue for the year ended 31 May 2026 for the UK arm was up 2 per cent to £5.81bn, with growth across all businesses.

The UK’s financial watchdog has proposed changes to retail investment fund rules in a bid to reduce the risk of rushed asset sales during market volatility.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) floated a minimum 90-day notice period for investors withdrawing from long-term investment funds holding illiquid assets such as infrastructure and private equity, in its latest consultation paper.

This would end current practices where funds allow clients to take money out daily with no notice period, leaving them vulnerable during times of market stress and volatility. 

Turbulent periods can often spark a sudden wave of investor withdrawal requests, leading fund managers to run out of enough liquid capital to satisfy the redemptions forcing them to suspend the fund.

An influx of withdrawals can also harm investors who are too slow to react, leaving them holding a frozen, illiquid fund.

Funds will only be able to process redemptions once per month, under the mooted plans, and the combined notice and settlement period will not be allowed to exceed 185 days.

Michelle Beck, director, markets, at the FCA, said: “Funds should be clear about whether they offer quick access or are built for longer-term investments like property.”

The Woodford legacy

Long-term investment funds have come under increased scrutiny from the watchdog in recent years, following the collapse of disgraced fund manager Neil Woodford’s Woodford Equity Income Fund (WEIF).

The fund – once one of the UK’s largest and most successful – was suspended in June 2019, leaving investors unable to access their money and trapping around £3.7bn in hard-to-sell assets in what was one of the most dramatic collapses in UK investment history.

The fund’s assets under management had fallen from a high of over £10.1bn in May 2017 to just £3.7bn in the run-up to its suspension.

The FCA concluded that between July 2018 and June 2019, Woodford “made unreasonable and inappropriate investment decisions”, disproportionately selling more liquid investments and buying less liquid ones.

By the time of the suspension, only eight per cent of investments held by WEIF could be sold within seven days.

This broke rules in place at the time, which stated investors should be able to access their funds in seven days.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has said that governments should look to help keep prices stable and win over markets with disinflationary tax and spending measures. 

In an intervention on the relationship between monetary and fiscal policy, Bailey urged governments to consider the impacts of government spending and borrowing on inflation.

The Bank of England chief, who is also the chair of the global Financial Stability Board, said governments should take decisions that commit to both price and financial stability. 

He added that it was not for him to “comment on fiscal policy and thereby cross the line beyond central banking”. 

In remarks given at the Istanbul Economic Forum, the monetary authority chief also called on governments to exercise fiscal restraint. “Whatever the stance of fiscal policy is, it must be credible and direct to that stability, and seen to be as such by markets.” 

“A continued commitment to the policy stance can then help to control the emergence of risk premia, something that is likely to happen otherwise when a major conflict in the Middle East breaks out. 

“Such commitments are needed more than ever when these negative shocks occur. Fiscal rules can have an important role to play in securing this outcome, just like inflation targets.”

Inflation to rise after Healey’s Budget

The Bank of England is mandated to keep CPI inflation at two per cent, with Bailey having to write to the Chancellor to explain why inflation has exceeded three per cent whenever it does. UK inflation in the 12 months to August was 3.1 per cent.

The Bank expects inflation to rise above four per cent in the coming months as the UK is exposed to sky-high global energy prices. The Brent crude, which is a marker for energy costs, jumped from $90 to over $100 a barrel in the last month. 

Bailey’s comments are timely reading for Chancellor John Healey ahead of the Budget later this month. Healey faces a battle in reining in government spending amid higher debt interest payments while also delivering support to households on the cost of living, as well as bosses on the cost of business. 

Bailey warned in his speech at the Istanbul Economic Forum that the longer energy prices remained high, the more “difficult” it would become for the Bank of England to see the situation as temporary. 

“[A] ‘look-through’ approach only works if inflation expectations stay anchored to target,” Bailey said.

“If households and firms start building this shock into their wage and price setting behaviour, this temporary effect quickly turns into a persistent effects.”

Speaking about the UK’s own problems, he added: “We are conscious that the history of recent years pointed to a risk of elevated inflation expectations.”

The Bank is widely expected to hike interest rates to four per cent at its next meeting a week after the Budget. 

Several top economists and global bankers have raised the alarm on high levels of government borrowing. The International Monetary Fund’s Kristalina Georgieva warned earlier this year that higher government debt levels are leaving countries vulnerable in an economic downturn. 

The 10-year gilt yield, the benchmark for UK government borrowing costs, has climbed from around 4.2 per cent in March this year to nearly 5.5 per cent, adding billions to Healey’s debt interest bill. 

Bailey said that high levels of leverage used for AI investments increased risks although markets had not become “disorderly”. 

“We can’t in any way be relaxed about the current state of financial markets,” he said.

The Midday Market report is a new newsletter from City AM, giving you fresh analysis on the biggest stories in the City straight into your inbox every lunchtime. Today, Ali Lyon chews over Kemi Badenoch’s Tory conference inheritance tax overhaul, and what it might mean for the UK’s irrational tax system. Sign up to the City AM News Updates newsletter here.

Can I invite you to cast your mind back to this time last year, when an embattled Kemi Badenoch – under threat from circling leadership hopefuls – stepped into the main auditorium at the Conservatives’ annual conference and gave her maiden speech as party leader.

You may recall that expectations among the chattering political classes were low. With the party languishing in the polls, then-Conservative frontbencher Robert Jenrick and former leadership hopeful James Cleverly were rumoured to be sharpening their knives waiting to pounce on any bum notes. The stakes could hardly have been higher.

In the end, though, a swaggering Badenoch swatted away that speculation over her position with aplomb, and left the Tory jamboree firmly on the front foot in the eyes of her party faithful. One of the main reasons for her doing so was an eye-catching promise to abolish stamp duty on homes – a pernicious tax that economists of almost all creeds despise.

Among tough competition, the levy, bolted on to house purchases at a rate of between two and 12 per cent, is held up as one of the most illogical and economically ruinous in HMRC’s armoury. It gums up the property market, stopping workers from taking jobs in parts of the country where they would earn more money and be more productive. And – crucially – it prevents empty-nesters from downsizing into a home more suited to a life without their little angels leaving the lights on and raiding the fridge.

In pledging to abolish it, the Conservatives had united economists and political commentators in a moment of rare agreement. Here was a party willing to grasp the nettle on property tax reform, and go for growth.

Inheritance tax overhaul could leave hot property even hotter

This year, with her position as leader far more assured, Badenoch attempted a similar ruse, and put another mightily unpopular levy on the scrap heap.

At the climax of her similarly well-received speech yesterday, the Tory leader promised that – if elected – her party would scrap all inheritance tax on ‘family homes’.

Passing on your home to your family, she argued, “is one of the most human instincts of all”. They are where we watch “our children take their first steps” and gather “every Christmas”, she said. Forcing a family to sell that home – and those memories – to foot a big inheritance tax bill was unconservative and, thus, for the chop.

It was, undoubtedly, a canny piece of political manoeuvring. Inheritance tax regularly tops the list of UK voters’ most hated levies. And, as the charts (courtesy of tax national treasure Dan Neidle) above and below make clear, those that stand to benefit most from the overhaul sit either in the Tory base or who in pockets of affluent London most likely to feel betrayed by Labour’s consecutive tax raids.

That, however, is where this newsletter’s praise for the hijinx ends. For where last year’s stamp duty promise managed to earn economic plaudits as well as political ones, this inheritance shake-up has only done the latter. Among their core objections, is the enormously distortive effect it will have on the UK’s moribund property market.

Remember, the stamp duty pledge was in part so well received because it would help couples downsize, freeing up the property market and encouraging transactions. This does the complete opposite. It encourages tax-savvy grannies to hold onto their homes – or even upsize in a world of no stamp duty – to minimise their inheritance tax exposure.

“If you want an IHT cut, this is just about the worst way to do it,” says London School of Economics tax guru, Andy Summers, branding it “perfectly calibrated to prevent downsizing and further gum up the housing market”.

Evelyn Partners’ Ian Dyall adds that it could even have the unintended consequence of “adding to upward pressure on prices” in a pocket of the property market where supply is already constrained.

The Conservative Party press release renounced inheritance tax as “morally wrong and a form of double taxation to take assets that people have purchased with money that attracted tax. But does this half-baked shake-up risk leaving our illogical, dysfunctional tax system even worse than it already is?

To the country’s army of tax lawyers, economists and financial planners, the answer to that question is, unequivocally, yes.

]]> 2464322Ali Lyon Ali Lyon MFS founder accuses administrators of ‘internecine warfare’ https://www.cityam.com/mfs-founder-accuses-administrators-of-internecine-warfare/ Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:32:09 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2464382

The founder of collapsed shadow bank MFS has accused administrators of “internecine warfare” and harassment as the firm’s creditors fight to unlock billions of pounds in frozen funds, City AM can reveal.  Paresh Raja, the chief executive of Market Financial Solutions who has denied claims he siphoned “vast sums” from the mortgage firm, has asked [...]]]>

The founder of collapsed shadow bank MFS has accused administrators of “internecine warfare” and harassment as the firm’s creditors fight to unlock billions of pounds in frozen funds, City AM can reveal. 

Paresh Raja, the chief executive of Market Financial Solutions who has denied claims he siphoned “vast sums” from the mortgage firm, has asked the High Court to force all competing claims against him into a single, coordinated process.

Raja is currently facing five separate proceedings from MFS entities that top £1.5bn. Amber Bridging and Zircon Bridging – the creditor companies that forced MFS into administration – are understood to be preparing a sixth claim, according to legal filings seen by City AM. 

“There appears to be a significant degree of internecine warfare, the effect of which has been to harass Mr Raja at every stage with increasingly ‘urgent’ applications and across a range of fora, as each entity seeks to get what it evidently perceives to be ‘ahead’ of the others,” lawyers representing Raja said in court filings.

The filings also accused administrators of “advancing competing, and overlapping and/or inconsistent, claims to what appears to be the same pool of money”.

MFS – which operated as a UK non-bank lender that funded its loan book through institutional debt facilities – collapsed into administration in February 2026, owing institutional lenders over £1.1bn. Raja has been accused of operating a double pledging scheme, whereby he allegedly used identical property assets as collateral for multiple, simultaneous loans from different major lenders, creating a major shortfall.

A source familiar with the matter said: “The multiplicity of claims is clearly a reflection of the case and the way in which [Raja] structured MFS”.

The fight for MFS’ cash

Multiple different administrators have been handed control of different special purpose vehicles in the MFS web of companies. The legal filings from Raja are in response to a claim from London Bridging Limited, which administrators from FRP have taken over. 

FRP are seeking to claw back around £51m in funds, which has been reduced from £242m previously. 

Administrators are also locked in a legal battle with Barclays to retrieve funds they claim belong to them that have been frozen by the bank. Barclays held a dual role in the MFS ecosystem, acting as both a lender and providing primary transactional bank activities.

City AM was the first to reveal Barclays was holding in excess of £160m belonging to the operating unit and silos at the time of the administration. It began freezing MFS accounts in November 2025 after spotting irregularities.

Raja has blamed the bank for the collapse of MFS, and in separate filings accused it of “paralysing” the business when it froze accounts.

Barclays has said it “acted at all times, and continues to act, in accordance with its legal and regulatory obligations”.

FRP declined to comment. Amber and Zircon declined to comment.

The NBA wants its European basketball competition to replicate the dynamic between football’s Champions League and Europa League. Much of the rest of the detail surrounding a property slated for launch next year remains under wraps.

A cloud may have fallen over talks between the NBA and EuroLeague but there is at least some welcome clarity on what a new European franchise competition operated by the US basketball behemoth will actually look like.

The vision for NBA Europe is a two-tier format based on football’s Champions League and Europa League model, the NBA’s managing director for Europe and the Middle East, George Aivazoglou, explained this week.

The 16-team top tier of a competition still slated for launch in 12 months’ time will be largely composed of new franchises in cities including London and Manchester alongside major clubs from the current European scene.

Four spaces will be open to qualification via a standalone tournament and performance in the second tier, which will be majority open based on domestic performance. The intended result is a united pyramid based on the European sports model.

“Our vision is to create a two-tier ecosystem, pan-European at the top,” Aivazoglou told the Sportico Invest London conference. 

“NBA Europe is a semi-open league, and then the second competition, the BCL [Basketball Champions League], will be fully open, so 75 per cent of the teams will come in a merit-based way. 

“In the last few months we’ve been very close in discussions with EuroLeague to figure out ways to bring them into our ecosystem. A lot of work is happening there, but the NBA’s intent is to work with the existing players who are in Europe.”

NBA insists on branding and eyes US-style governance

The NBA is determined to lure the likes of Real Madrid and Barcelona from EuroLeague and it would be far less messy – and more commercially viable – to do a deal with the incumbent competition.  

Those talks have been long-running and appeared to hit another bump this week when a meeting of EuroLeague chiefs in Italy is believed to have resulted in the rejection of the NBA’s latest proposal for a collaboration. 

The NBA says it favours cooperation but intends to launch in autumn 2027 regardless of the outcome of the discussions. EuroLeague has been open to collaboration but is advancing its own expansion plans in parallel. 

Reports this week reflected concerns that NBA Europe could be delayed until 2028, although Aivazoglou insinsted today that they were “moving ahead with our plans for a launch in the next year”.

With the clock ticking on the proposed start date and some prospective investors in new franchises, which the NBA believes will fetch $1bn in some markets, impatient for some clarity, decision time would appear to be approaching.

Neither the NBA nor EuroLeague has been prepared to comment on whether further talks will take place, although the feeling among insiders is that this isn’t the end of the road for an effective takeover by the NBA. Yet.

It is understood that the NBA is willing to discuss tweaks to the model and the BCL name – currently in use by its partner Fiba, the world governing body, for its pan-continental competition – but won’t budge on it being branded an NBA competition.

The NBA is also keen to replicate the governance structure in the US, defined by salary cap rules and collective bargaining agreements, as far as European laws allow.

NBA Europe will be global like Champions League

“The good news about it being the NBA is we know what the NBA looks like,” Josh Empson, a partner at private equity firm Sixth Street said this week. 

“Does the NBA in Europe look exactly like the NBA in the US? No. Does it look something more like the way the Champions League looks like in football, if that were a persistent year-round league where you’re playing across markets and across territories?

“Markets in Europe are obviously more different than states or cities are in the US and I think that’s one thing that’s exciting about this – we get that same energy of national competition that we see in the Champions League in football. I think that’s what a successful NBA Europe looks like, crossing those boundaries.”

Aivazoglou added: “For me, it’s two dimensions, going along the lines of Josh’s thinking, this will be something that will feel very natively European, very authentic. It will respect the traditions of the game. The game is being played and enjoyed in a very different way here than in the US.

“We want to keep it traditional and authentic, and keep the soul as it is, but bring in entertainment elements that allow different segments, different audiences to come in, and that is one of the big opportunities for European basketball. 

“The second component, this will be global if it’s successful, which I think it will be. It will be a global brand and platform. It will transcend Europe. It will feel original in the sense of the European psyche, but it will transcend it in the same way that the NBA transcends the US.”

Top housebuilders have begun to pull out of London citing a “nightmare” of planning objections that have made developments unviable.

Listed housebuilders Taylor Wimpey and Berkeley Group both said that the costs of navigating the huge complexities of red tape and planning processes in the capital are making them less willing to continue investing.

This week, a judge rejected Berkeley’s appeal against the rejection of its plans to build 867 new homes on the site of a shopping centre in Peckham. 

The housebuilder’s Aylesham Centre redevelopment was initially rejected on heritage grounds, and Southwark Council’s celebration of the decision was slammed as “downright offensive” by industry figures. 

Berkeley claims the project would have created 1,000 jobs and 60 apprenticeships, as well as generating more than £13m in extra annual spending in the area.

The housebuilder held six rounds of public consultation and 300 separate meetings with key stakeholders about its plans for the site, which has been earmarked for development since 2014.

Case for housebuilding ‘evaporates’

Rob Perrins, Berkeley’s executive chair, said heritage objections are being used as “a blocker” by planning inspectors and local authorities.

“This 10-year planning nightmare demonstrates the gulf between positive planning policies and what actually happens when you try to build homes in London. All the policies support housing, but the decisions block it time and time again,” he said.

Another key London development for the housebuilder, the Motspur Park Gasworks in Kingston, has been put on hold by the government despite already being approved by London mayor Sadiq Khan.

Thousands of Brits who saved into a Lifetime ISA were hit with multiple withdrawal penalties in a single tax year, as calls for the government to ensure the replacement product is fit for purpose grows.

Roughly 45,000 savers were penalised for unauthorised withdrawals from Lifetime ISAs (LISA) in the 2024/25 tax year, according to an FOI request from financial app Plum to HMRC.

The average saver penalised more than once lost roughly £760, as 33,530 were hit with fines ranging up to £999.

Nearly 4,000 Brits incurred fines in excess of £2,000, while 60 were slapped with charges surpassing a staggering £8,000.

“These are significant sums of money for first-time buyers who already face considerable obstacles to getting a foot on the housing ladder,” said Rajan Lakhani of Plum.

Brits who suffered multiple LISA penalties accounted for around a third of the 129,200 people penalised that tax year.

‘Flawed and outdated’

The LISA has been subjected to mass scrutiny and criticism in recent years, as banks and asset managers called out “flawed and outdated” rules.

The savings product  was launched in April 2017 by the Conservative government, allowing individuals aged 18 to 40 to contribute £4,000 tax free each year, to either put towards a first home or retirement.

But many have called out the scheme arguing they are unable to benefit as the product’s property price has been frozen at £450,000 since its introduction, despite house inflation.

This has locked out many buyers in London and the South East. The average house price hit £531,548 in September, according to figures from the Official of National Statistics.

Purchasing a home above this cap is classified as an unauthorised withdrawal, triggering the penalty. Holders are subject to a 25 per cent penalty on the total withdrawn, including the government bonus and their own money, causing many to have less than originally started.

Savers putting in £1,000 would receive a bonus of 25 per cent making their pot worth £1,250. But if they withdrew that £1,250 in cash they would lose £312.50, leaving them with £937.50.

New Lifetime Isa product battle

Lakhani said the loss of significant sums has caused people to shift their focus to ensuring the new First Time Buyer ISA is “fit for purpose”.

Plans for replacing the LISA were first outlined in former chancellor Rachel Reeves’ 2025 Autumn Budget, before confirming the new product would be introduced in a consultation published by the Treasury in June. The government conceded the product was “not working well for many” and “putting off some savers”.

The new product, which is yet to be given an official launch date by the government, is expected to remove the option of using funds for retirement and add the bonus only when a saver is ready to purchase a property. It will also have no upper age limit.

It will also eliminate cash withdrawal penalties which many would-be first-time buyers may have felt necessary to cover day-to-day living expenses. 

But providers are urging the government to remove the national cap in favour of a regional one, reflecting how price inflation is hitting different areas of the UK, while others, including Plum, have called for the national limit to be increased to roughly £600,000.

Lakhani said: “First-time buyers in London and the South East face the most acute affordability challenges in the country. The effect of the existing Lifetime ISA… has shut many out of the housing market altogether.”

But some firms have argued the Lifetime ISA should not be replaced, calling instead for improvements to the existing product, arguing the shake-up will add further complexity.

“The Lifetime ISA…needs targeted improvements,including to the withdrawal penalty and house-price cap, but these changes can be made now for the people already relying on it,” said Moneybox’s Brian Byrnes.

“We should not replace a product that is already helping people buy a home with a new first-time buyer ISA. Nor should people already relying on the Lifetime ISA have to wait until 2028 for much-need improvements to the product.”

Timekettle LiveTalk | £129 | timekettle.co

There are certain technologies that feel innately futuristic, the stuff of science fiction, the kind of thing we terrestrial mortals probably shouldn’t have access to. Some of these, like video calls, are now mainstream. Others, like flying cars and robot butlers, are still some way off. And others walk a tightrope between these two poles. Live translation between languages fits into this category: it exists, but in a nascent enough form that it still feels like it shouldn’t.

It’s been around in some form for a few years but, as tends to be the case with these things, came into most people’s consciousness when Apple included it as a feature in its AirPods. And it works… kind of. Your AirPods have access to nine languages and translation is… rudimentary. It gets the job done, provided the job is getting directions to the piscine or ordering patatas bravas. It struggles with accents.

This is where the Timekettle LiveTalk comes in, promising to move us one step closer to the Babel Fish from The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. There’s something a retro about these earbuds, coming in a clamshell case and made from a white translucent plastic, which looks like how people probably imagined the future would look before it arrived. They feature a discreet earbud with a coil that wraps above your ear. They’re lightweight and relatively comfortable – I’m wearing them as I type this and can barely tell I have them in. They will function as regular earphones but you should absolutely not use them for this purpose, the sound being a bit like when you put earbuds inside a glass to try and make a caveman-style speaker.

The Timekettle LiveTalk tested

What they do much better is translation, for which they use AI to parse what you’re saying and translate it on the trot. The great thing about the LiveTalk is the breadth of languages included: 52 in total, with 106 accents catered for. I started off using the “One earbud shared” option with my friend Joe, one of City AM’s videographers, who has family in Hong Kong. It works like this: each of you puts in an earbud, selects the languages you want to translate (English and Cantonese) and… you just start talking.

To begin with, things did not go well: there’s a fairly long delay between the original speech and the translation – around five seconds – which takes a bit of getting used to. Once you adapt to this, things get better: translating to and from Cantonese is no mean feat so the translation is understandably pretty basic. But we managed to have a short conversation about what we did last night – Joe went to the pub and I… also went to the pub. It struggled to identify proper nouns, instead making ‘informed’ guesses, which were sometimes kind of close and other times hilariously far from the mark. Joe reckoned this might be down to his Hong Kong accent  – I have no idea if Hong Kong is included in the 106 regional accents but this sounds plausible.

More successful was translating to and from Spanish. Another of our videographers, Joey, has family from Ecuador and he was surprised to see the LiveTalk has a specific option for Ecuadorian Spanish, where most translation software uses the broader “Latin American”. We were able to have a perfectly decent chat about the guests on City AM’s afternoon podcast, the preparation for which I had just interrupted. Again, the time delay takes a bit of getting used to but I can imagine using this when travelling in South America and getting by just fine. 

Another option is to live translate a voice call, which also works well, with the same caveats; expect a delay. I’m yet to test the ‘live listening’ feature – put them in and it will translate whatever it picks up – but I’ll update this review next time I go abroad (I’m sceptical the AI could keep up with multiple inputs at once but I’m prepared to be proven wrong).

The Timekettle LiveTalk earbuds work better than I had expected and only slightly worse than I had hoped. This kind of accuracy, however, comes at a cost: you get 200 free minutes of translation a month but beyond that you have to pay: £9.99 a month gets you unlimited translation with lower tiers also available. If you travel often, upgrading feels like a no-brainer, at least until Apple’s version catches up (it’s currently free).

This kind of tech is still young and while £129 won’t exactly break the bank, it’s a not insignificant outlay for something that’s likely to improve exponentially over the coming years. But if you’re a regular traveller who needs translation that’s a cut above the more basic options on the market, these should absolutely be on your radar.

Ride-hailing platform Bolt has been refused permission to appeal a case brought by HMRC over how it calculates and pays its VAT.

This follows HMRC winning an appeal in June against the Estonian tech giant over its VAT payments and calculations, overturning earlier decisions that had ruled in Bolt’s favour.

The tax authority brought the appeal, questioning whether Bolt could use the tour operators’ margin scheme (TOMS). Under this scheme, businesses only pay VAT on the profit margin they make between buying a service and selling it to the customer. By qualifying for this scheme, Bolt must account for VAT only on the commission it takes from the fare, rather than the entire gross fare paid by the passenger.

Bolt’s appeal involves an estimated £190m in unpaid VAT.

HMRC had argued in February 2023 that Bolt did not qualify for this scheme, and the Court of Appeal backed the tax authority’s decision.

Bolt sought to appeal to the top court, but the Supreme Court refused Bolt’s appeal application, saying it “does not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance which the Supreme Court ought to hear at this time.”

Commenting on the decision, Kimberly Hurd, senior general manager for the UK and Ireland at Bolt, said in a statement: “Two courts have already found in Bolt’s favour on this question. We are therefore disappointed that the Supreme Court has refused permission for Bolt to appeal the Court of Appeal’s findings.”

“Businesses need a tax framework that supports a competitive market. This has consequences for fares, for driver earnings and for consumer choice across the sector that earlier rulings provided – supporting the 100,000 drivers that earn through our platform, and the millions of passengers that have depended on affordable and accessible transport,” Hurd added.

Bolt generated €2.27bn (£1.92bn) in revenue in 2025, and the UK is the firm’s second-biggest market.

Decision may bring Uber case ‘to a close’

Sue Rathmell, VAT partner at MHA, said the decision “brings to an end a long-running dispute.”

“Under TOMS, VAT is only payable on the operator’s margin rather than the full value of the fare. HMRC has argued for several years that the scheme was never intended to apply to ride-hailing businesses, while operators maintained that they were entitled to use it under the existing legislation,” Rathmell said.

Ride-hailing giant Uber has a similar ongoing legal battle over a £1bn VAT bill over TOMS, awaiting to be heard by the Tax Tribunal, which this decision could impact.

The court said in its judgment in June that other cases, including Uber’s, ”are awaiting its [Bolt’s case’s] outcome.”

“The Supreme Court’s decision to refuse Bolt permission to appeal means HMRC’s victory at the Court of Appeal now stands. Uber’s case was effectively waiting in the wings behind Bolt, so this decision is likely to bring the wider litigation to a close,” Rathmell said.

Black cab drivers already urged that the government to close this tax loophole used by Uber and Bolt, writing to the Chancellor last November asking her to make the tech ride-hailing apps pay the same level of VAT as cabbies.

HMRC was contacted for comment.

At their party conference in Birmingham, the Tories tried their best to bring back the good times. Reporters who have been following the Conservatives for years privately joked that the labyrinth conference centre had about a third of the amount of people as when the party was in government. Young Conservatives were paraded as future stars in several events although even then the vibes in the day were somewhat off. Just ask shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith, who waited for quiet applause to fade out before awkwardly walking off stage after his main speech. Or deputy leader Alex Burghart, who mistakenly said Sir Niall Ferguson had visited Russia in a panel event when he had in fact travelled to Kyiv. But the Tories are not really day people anyway. The waiting time for pints at the conference’s hotel lobby was no less than 20 minutes at times. The LGBT+ Conservatives threw a party for the ages, featuring MPs such as Blake Stephenson and Katie Lam, and James McAlpine, the world’s tallest Tory at a height of 7ft 2in, dancing to hits from the ‘80s. Some hacks got in the spirit of fun with a breakaway to karaoke. It’s in the late hours of the night that staffers and activists really feel like they’ve been sent back to the glory days.

FREE-FOR-ALL AT THE TREASURY
What’s going on at the Treasury? Even life-long critics recognise that the best and brightest are found there, but are standards slipping? John Healey’s department is advertising for a pensions policy adviser to “lead and co-ordinate HMT’s input to the Pensions Commission”, and before you rule yourself out, consider that “You do not need to be a policy professional or have any specific qualifications to succeed in the role.” HMT has also launched its 2027 Graduate Policy Programme, offering a three year stint to aspiring economic policy wonks. The ad makes clear that a degree in economics is not required, and that it’s open to anyone with a 2:2 degree in any subject. Brightest and best, step up!

A BOOZY NIGHT AT THE BAYEUX TAPESTRY
Apparently some members of the public with tickets to see the Bayeux Tapestry (as opposed to the Tory version) have been hampered by painfully long queues, with some left out in the cold entirely. No such hardship for guests at media tycoon Mike Bloomberg’s annual party at the British Museum last night, with a seamless parade of political, media and City bigwigs able to enjoy the Norman embroidery at their leisure. Alas, the gin cocktails had to be left outside the viewing gallery but we’re happy to report that fresh glasses were on offer at the exit.

SLUMMING IT
The Tories have been showcasing their plans for spending cuts at their conference this week and The Capitalist hears they aren’t just talking the talk. One thrifty shadow cabinet member booked a shared room in a hostel with a loo down the corridor. Another struggled to identify himself after losing his key. “Burnham’s Burmigham” one of our correspondents quipped…

BELGRAVIA MEMBERS’ CLUB CUTS THE FAT
News that private members’ club The Pembroke was hiring a “butter sommelier” sparked intrigue earlier this year. A novel way, indeed, to put bread on the table. Sadly, the club confirmed to us that they didn’t “move forward” with the hire, despite The Guardian this week pronouncing that we are in the age of the great “butter boom”. A slippery story indeed.
